items.title: Nepal: Predatory Lending Abuses Exacerbated by Conflict in the Gulf
items.description: Click to expand Image Loan shark victims demand justice after 38 days of protest in Kathmandu, Nepal, March 7, 2024. © 2024 Skanda Gautam/SOPA Images/Sipa via AP Photo Thousands of borrowers face exorbitant interest on fraudulent loan agreements taken out to fund labor migration and other needs.The Nepali government has criminalized abusive practices, but police and courts often side with loan sharks against distressed borrowers.Lost job opportunities due to war in the Gulf region have deepened the crisis facing many borrowers. (Tokyo) – Authorities in Nepal should hold illegal moneylenders accountable for abuses against borrowers, including unlawful land dispossession, arbitrary eviction, threats and acts of violence, and sexual exploitation, Human Rights Watch said today. Conflicts in the Gulf region, where many Nepalis are migrant workers facing exorbitant recruitment fees, have made more people vulnerable to extortion by illegal lenders. “Despite government commitments to protect borrowers, illegal practices are rife in Nepal’s informal credit sector, leaving those with the fewest resources dependent on moneylenders who can take everything they own,” said Meenakshi Ganguly, Asia deputy director at Human Rights Watch. “The government of Prime Minister Balendra Shah should carry out the government’s commitments to ensure that the law against fraudulent and abusive lending is consistently enforced.” Human Rights Watch interviewed 18 borrowers, as well as local government officials, lawyers, and activists from six districts in the Terai region where informal money lending is rampant, reviewed government reports, and examined over 50 cases in Nawalparasi district. Human Rights Watch found that many families are struggling with unmanageable debt particularly as migrant workers in the Gulf States during 2026 have faced reduced incomes or involuntary travel delays ahead of starting jobs due to the conflict between the US, Israel, and Iran. War-induced disruption amplified pre-existing abuses, including reliance on unauthorized individual agents and unreasonable recruitment fees. Human Rights Watch previously found that companies in Gulf states play a critical role in driving these illegal costs by refusing to cover costs and fees to recruiters that they know will be borne by workers. Government investigations have shown that, under Nepal’s informal credit practices, a borrower signs or thumbprints an unsecured personal loan contract, known locally as kapali tamasuk, which can falsely list a principal amount three to ten times more than the cash received. These loans, known as meter byaj, in some cases compound at annual rates ranging from 36 percent to 60 percent or more, compared with less than 10 percent charged by banks. As low-income households that had relied on remittances disrupted by the war have shifted their limited resources toward expenses for food, fuel, and healthcare, they have been increasingly unable to repay their loans, leading to a surge in defaults. In response, some moneylenders are forcing evictions or land transfers, including through violence, in the worst cases tying people into generational debt. Nepal authorities are not pushing for effective long term solutions beyond encouraging and facilitating debtors and creditors to enter pre-court settlements. Following the outbreak of conflict in the Persian Gulf, in March 2026, the Nepal government suspended both institutional and individual labor permits to protect its citizens, including to Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, and Kuwait, with an estimated 2,000 Nepalis denied labor permits daily. Thousands were stopped from travelling at the international airport despite possessing valid medical clearances, verified visas, and binding employment contracts, while administrative delays also led foreign firms to cancel labor contracts. However, the authorities failed to step in to protect aspiring migrant laborers who still had to service their high interest meter byaj loans, leaving them exposed to violent enforcement by loan sharks. “They did not just hit my father to get the money,” said one victim. “They beat him in the middle of the road during the day so that everyone else in the village would see what happens when you cannot pay the meter byaj. The local goons told us, ‘If you don’t sign over the land title today, your family will receive a corpse tomorrow.’” While abuses, including violent attacks and forced evictions, appear to be increasing due to conflict related disruptions, many moneylenders have long wielded political and economic power over borrowers. Claiming that the justice system routinely favors the moneylenders, borrowers have staged three extended protests in Kathmandu over the last four years—the longest for 442 days—and three long marches. Each time, the government agreed to resolve debt issues but failed to honor its commitments to protect victims. Consequently, the borrowers have regularly protested at district and provincial levels as well. Although government has criminalized such loans, borrowers and activists in Madhesh Province said that police have repeatedly refused to file reports when victims seek protection. Instead, they said, the police typically dismiss abuses and intimidation by moneylenders as “private civil disputes.” “When the moneylender came to break our door, we ran to the police, but the officers told us to go home and settle personal transactional disputes ourselves,” said a Rautahat district migrant worker. The police also back moneylenders when they use signed blank checks and banking laws to threaten defaulters with arrest, or use informal deeds as the basis to seize land and evict families. “The lender made me sign a blank check when he gave me a loan, and later on he filled it for 10 lakhs (US$6,500) and sent the police to threaten me with jail when the check bounced,” said a Siraha district farmer. Borrowers also cite cases in which the authorities do not intervene even when lenders use patently unlawful loan agreements to obtain asset foreclosure orders. “The lender told me openly that he owns the courts and the administration,” said Shiv Shanker from Gaur, Rautahat district, who after facing abuses from a moneylender, is leading protests. “When the state shuts its doors on a poor farmer, death feels like the only place left to hide from this meter byaj.” On May 5, 2023, the government criminalized informal loans as an “improper transaction,” and declared that forging loan contracts, threatening borrowers, or fabricating loan amounts, are punishable by up to seven years in prison. However, enforcement remains weak. Successive governments have established inquiry commissions to address the crisis, but over 65,000 complaints registered with inquiry commissions remain unresolved due to a lack of legal provisions and administrative bottlenecks. These failures have contributed to deadly outcomes including suicide. Santidevi Mahato from Biratnagar died by suicide on June 21, following threats from a moneylender because she could not service her debt, people interviewed said. After borrowing 150,000 Nepali rupees (US$975) in October 2015, she had repaid 400,000 Nepali rupees (US$2,600) in installments. Yet, violating their agreement, the moneylender seized her land and threatened to evict her from her house. Under international human rights law and standards, governments have the obligation to take steps to protect people from serious rights abuses caused by private actors, such as moneylenders, including through investigating and prosecuting serious crimes. On July 17, the government led by Prime Minister Balendra Shah concluded a nine-point pact with protest leaders to eliminate predatory lending, after debt victims began a march to Kathmandu. The government should take immediate legal and policy steps to institutionalize its commitment, Human Rights Watch said. Nepal’s donors and international partners should assist the government to establish systematic debt relief, and grievance mechanisms that can support debt restructuring. “The Balendra Shah government was elected with the promise of change, to overturn existing oppressive structures,” Ganguly said. “More closely regulating moneylenders and ending their chokehold on farmers and laborers is a crucial step in ensuring lasting social justice.” Loan Sharks and Migrant Workers from Nepal Nepal’s informal credit system is rooted in its feudal history, where local elites used predatory debt to trap peasants in tenancy and systems of generational servitude such as Kamaiya, Haliya, and Haruwa-Charuwa. The present-day meter byaj system evolved around a spurt in labor migration during the decade-long civil war in Nepal, from 1996 to 2006, and rapidly spread after the 2007 political unrest in the Terai region. An estimated 7 million Nepalis work abroad, about half in India and a majority of the rest in Gulf countries, contributing a third of the national GDP. For many households, migration became one of the few viable ways to earn a living, while the absence of accessible and affordable institutional credit left them dependent on informal lenders to finance the costs of securing employment abroad. Some local moneylenders and corrupt agents demanded exorbitant fees to help rural youth find jobs abroad, particularly in the Gulf States and Malaysia. Land or property was borrowers’ main collateral, but they often later discovered that their contracts were fraudulent, including falsified sums and forged documents. The schemes exploited bureaucratic complicity at government land offices to transfer property titles despite contracts being illegal, and borrowers lost their assets due to a lack of protection from the government. In interviews, debt victims described devastating cycles in which migrant workers are forever bound to serving a predatory moneylender, while the authorities fail to intervene. Ramnath Musahar from Susta, Nawalparasi district, said the family borrowed to send two of his brothers to work in the Gulf States in 2015, but despite servicing the loan, their debt had grown enormously: My brothers sent back Rs. 1,200,000 (US$8,000) from their wages, and we sold our plots [of land] to pay an extra Rs. 1,800,000 (US$11,000). But the lender went to the district court with a fake contract and claimed we still owe him Rs. 5,000,000 (US$33,000). The court looked only at the paper and our thumbprints; it did not look at our tears. The police came and threw our belongings into the dirt. We went from being independent farmers to beggars overnight. Conflict Between the US, Israel, and Iran Exacerbates Debt Risks Since the US and Israel began their assault on Iran on February 28, 2026, and Iran subsequently blocked and attacked ships traveling through the Strait of Hormuz and attacked sites across the Gulf States, the fallout is being felt far beyond the region. In Nepal, UN agencies warned that “rising fuel prices, closure of shipping routes, and growing financial uncertainty are placing mounting pressure on economies, labor markets and vulnerable households.” According to the World Bank, Nepal’s real GDP growth could fall from 3.67 percent in 2024 to 2.3 percent in 2026 due to reduced tourism, higher transport costs, and supply chain snags. Rising inflation, a weakening currency leading to a rise in import costs, a spike in fuel costs, and stalled fertilizer supply have placed additional pressure on low-income households, and increased demands for overseas employment. Hoping to seek jobs to support their families, many rural youths have taken loans from loan sharks, who have responded by raising rates. Many families were stuck servicing those loans, even as people were unable to travel because of conflict-related disruptions. Workers already employed in the Gulf States are facing job losses, unpaid leave, wage reductions, and other disruptions that have reduced their ability to keep sending remittances. Compared with the same period the previous year, Gulf-bound labor approvals plummeted by 52 percent—from 228,165 down to 109,249—between the outbreak of the war in late February and mid-September, according to Department of Foreign Employment data. At least two Nepali workers have been killed due to the conflict, and 15 injured. Many are returning to Nepal stripped of their anticipated income, and unable to service their loans. The authorities have failed to act as moneylenders crack down on defaulters, beating them, evicting them, and forcing land or asset transfers. The lenders are also seeking court-ordered asset foreclosures and even arrest warrants based on the loan contracts, including contracts that borrowers alleged contained fabricated loan amounts. As a Mahotari district borrower observed, “The law says meter byaj is a crime, but police demanded receipts I never got, so the thief walks free, and I am made the criminal.” Women-led households, Dalits (considered an “untouchable” caste), and Indigenous ethnic communities have even fewer protections from violence such as beatings and sexual violence due to their caste, gender, and discrimination. One woman from Dhanusha district said she was raped by a moneylender under threat of eviction. My husband was trapped in a labor camp abroad and couldn’t send money. The lender came to my house with the contract and said he would evict my children the next morning unless I “compromised” with him. He held our roof over my head like a weapon. I had to endure his abuse in silence because a poor woman in this village has no voice against a powerful man who holds her land paper. Abuses by Moneylenders While the conflict has exacerbated the crisis, debt-ridden families had already proliferated in Nepal, particularly in Terai districts. The authorities have failed to protect these families. Chirai Chamar, a widowed Dalit worker in Paklihawa, Nawalparasi district, while struggling to gain control of her inherited family land, had borrowed 20,000 Nepali rupees (US$130). A moneylender offered to help with the legalities in exchange for a portion of that land. “A moneylender, from whom I had borrowed Rs. 20,000, came to me saying he will help me to acquire all the papers required to own my family land, and in return I need to give him two katthas (650 square meters) of land,” she said. He then grabbed an additional four katthas (1336 square meters), paying Chamar a grossly undervalued sum of Rs. 150,000 (US$970). When rights activists intervened to reclaim Chamar’s land and restore her livelihood, local thugs threatened them and destroyed Chamar’s crops. Despite complaints, the police and the local officials failed to assist her. Ashamaya (name changed), a resident of Thecho, Lalitpur, supported her family by running a small tea shop. However, when her father-in-law fell ill, she had to close the business to care for him. Left without income as the medical expenses mounted, she borrowed money from a moneylender, who charged an extortionate annual interest rate of 120 percent, which she could not pay. Under pressure, she took on another usurious loan simply to pay off the old one. Although she settled that debt by selling a piece of land, she had to borrow again, this time to cover her husband’s medical costs, but she no longer had enough land for collateral. The moneylender coerced her into sex with multiple men after he forced her to sign a new contact for Rs. 2500,000 (UDS$16,167), amounting to five times her initial debt. Seeking a Remedy Debt victims have started to organize under various banners and groups, demanding that the government protect them from abusive loan sharks. In 2022, after hundreds walked barefoot for weeks from districts including Siraha, Dhanusha, Mahottari, Sarlahi, Kapilvastu, and Nawalparasi to stage protests in Kathmandu, the government at that time establisheda three-member Commission for the Investigation of Loan Sharking (CILS) in April 2023, to collect complaints, study structural issues, and resolve loan-sharking disputes. By May 21, 2023, when the District Administration Offices stopped accepting these complaints, over 28,000 had been filed across 67 districts, with an alarming 21,552 cases concentrated in Madhesh Province. However, the commission only resolved and closed 5,115 loan disputes. Several victims reported abuses by district offices. “We went to the Chief District Officer expecting justice, but instead, the police and the lender ganged up on us, warned us that going to court would mean total land auction, and scared us into signing an agreement to pay half the inflated sum,” said a woman from Siraha. As complaints persisted, including of violent encounters in which the police failed to intervene, the authorities largely resorted to symbolic agreements with the victims, followed by the repeated formation of new commissions. A commission was set up in March 2024, led by former high court judge Tej Bahadur Karki, and another in March 2025, led by Baburam Regmi. In November 2025, the Regmi Commission reported a total of 41,409 complaints registered in 43 districts. Of these, 6,393 cases had been resolved, while 35,016 complaints remain pending. Each commission exposed the vast scale of the crisis but political commitments to break the stranglehold of moneylenders remain unfulfilled. Nawalparasi’s Deputy Chief District Officer Poshan Raj Bhandari told Human Rights Watch that, “The existing law will not be enough to resolve this problem; the government needs to think of a separate legal process to resolve this.” When Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s government was elected in March 2026 with a large majority, victims had cause for hope. However, instead of the government ensuring a collective debt moratorium, victims say that moneylenders have convinced the police to issue a surge of arrest warrants against debtors. In response, victims have organized new protests. Nigra Nabin, a leader of the protest movement, said that based on “past experiences” the victims “had three long-standing demands” including the nullification of all illegal agreements and the underlying loan contracts that support them; a new law to institutionalize these actions and establish special legal procedures; and a separate entity dedicated to ensuring justice for the victims. On July 9, the anti-loan shark movement began an 11-day justice march from Janakpur to Kathmandu. On the sixth day of the march, Home Affairs Minister Sudhan Gurung traveled to Nijgadh to hold direct talks with the protesters. Following three days of negotiations, the government accepted the three core demands and signed an updated nine-point deal, leading the protesters to call off the march. The victims are waiting. One of them, Sobita Devi Mahato, said: “If this is not resolved, the only resort I have is to go to the Home Ministry and hang myself there.” RecommendationsHalt arbitrary arrests of borrowers.Prosecute exploitative lenders for crimes against defaulters including violent attacks, sexual exploitation, and threats.Impose penalties for predatory lending practices, including aggressive debt collection through forced eviction or land grabs.Stop district authorities and police from carrying out foreclosures and evictions based on illegal loan agreements.Draft a new law to end illegal loan agreements and usury-related abuses. Establish a legal hold on all land transfers and evictions tied to disputed informal loans.Provide assistance, including debt relief where possible, to migrant workers in crisis because of sudden loss of work due to circumstances beyond their control, including war.Devise and enforce laws and policies that are designed to protect borrowers, including interest rate caps, requirements that borrowers have full and clear information about loan terms, and proper assessment of borrowers’ ability to repay loans. Consult with victims and stakeholders while drafting new laws and policies to dismantle the abusive informal moneylending system.Expand access to affordable institutional credit for low-income households and strengthen oversight of labor recruitment so that workers are not forced to rely on abusive informal lenders to finance migration or other essential expenses.Expand access to decent work and livelihoods in Nepal and strengthen social security so that households are less likely to rely on debt-financed labor migration.Use bilateral labor instruments such as labor agreements with governments of destination countries to ensure that companies hiring Nepali migrant workers cover the costs and fees related to their recruitment as per the employer pays principle, conduct proper due diligence and effective monitoring of Nepali recruiters, and have reimbursement mechanisms in instances when workers have paid fees.

items.title: BoG failed to adequately consult Parliament on new cedi notes — Tiah Mahama
items.description: The Bank of Ghana (BoG) has been criticised for failing to adequately engage Parliament in the process leading to the introduction of the new heritage series cedi banknotes. The Member of Parliament for Walewale, Dr Tiah Abdul Kabiru Mahama, said although the central bank had indicated that consultations on the currency redesign had been ongoing for two years, lawmakers were not sufficiently involved in the discussions. He said the limited engagement with Parliament was a major shortcoming in an exercise involving the country’s national currency, which represents its sovereignty and heritage. Speaking on Joy FM’s PM Express on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, Dr Mahama argued that the Bank of Ghana should have made a greater effort to involve MPs, given their responsibility to represent their constituents and help educate the public on national policy decisions. “I think that members of Parliament have not been brought along in terms of the cost and even the consultation,” he said. He acknowledged that the BoG had explained that it had undertaken consultations over the past two years before settling on the new notes but, questioned why elected representatives had not been sufficiently involved. “For me, the takeaway from this whole exercise is that the people’s representatives were not fully immersed in this consultation,” he said. Dr Mahama said engaging Parliament would have provided an effective channel for reaching citizens across the country, since MPs could convey information to their constituents and help explain the rationale for the changes. He also stressed that decisions concerning the national currency should be approached without partisan considerations, given their importance to the country’s identity and economic sovereignty. “Anything to ensure the sanctity of our currency, anything to ensure that our currency in fact has all the security features of international repute, or our currency is able to stand the test of time and durability – our currency marks our sovereignty and heritage,” he said. The MP, who is also a member of Parliament’s Finance Committee, said he only gained a better understanding of the currency redesign after an opportunity to discuss the matter with officials of the Bank of Ghana on the sidelines of an IMF meeting. He maintained that the committee established to oversee the exercise could have done more to engage Parliament. Under Parliament’s revised committee arrangements, operational matters relating to the Bank of Ghana fall under the Economy and Development Committee, while the Finance Committee retains responsibility for matters concerning the central bank’s budget and appropriation. Dr Mahama distinguished the new currency redesign from the routine printing of banknotes to replace worn-out notes and maintain adequate currency in circulation. He said the central bank had traditionally briefed Parliament on the recurring costs associated with currency replacement, usually through its budget or expenditure reports. However, he considered the introduction of the new heritage series a more extensive exercise that required broader engagement with lawmakers. The Bank of Ghana has introduced the heritage series as part of efforts to reflect Ghana’s history and identity through its national currency. The redesign has generated public discussion, including questions about its cost, consultation process and the reasons for the changes.

items.title: Mahama donates GH¢600,000 towards funeral of Agogomanhene
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has contributed GH¢600,000 towards the funeral of the late Agogomanhene, Nana Kwame Akuoko Sarpong, in recognition of the traditional ruler’s long service to the Agogo traditional area and the country. The donation was announced by the Ashanti Regional Minister, Dr Frank Amoakohene, who represented the President at the funeral observances in Agogo on Wednesday, November 25, 2026. Dr Amoakohene said the President had initially donated GH¢500,000 on Tuesday, November 24, before adding another GH¢100,000 the following day, bringing his total contribution to GH¢600,000. He conveyed the President’s condolences to the bereaved family and the people of Agogo, while paying tribute to the late chief’s contributions to national development. President Mahama also joined traditional rulers, family members and other mourners on the second day of the three-day Dɔte Yie observance to honour the memory of the late traditional leader. The lying-in-state, which began on Tuesday, has drawn mourners from different walks of life, including chiefs, religious leaders, public officials and members of the public, to pay their final respects. Nana Akuoko Sarpong, who ascended the Agogo stool in 1975, died on March 26, 2026, bringing to a close a 51-year reign marked by both traditional leadership and public service. His contribution to national life extended beyond the traditional council. During the Provisional National Defence Council (PNDC) era, he held several government positions, including Secretary for Health, Secretary for Internal Affairs and Secretary for Chieftaincy Affairs. He later served on the Council of State under the late President John Evans Atta Mills and was also associated with the formation of the National Democratic Congress (NDC). The funeral observances are scheduled to end on Thursday, November 26, 2026, in Agogo in the Ashanti Region.

items.title: Wole Olanipekun on law, democracy and the limits of power
items.description: By Ikechukwu Nnochiri Chief Wole Olanipekun (SAN), former Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice of old Ondo State, former President of the Nigerian Bar Association (NBA) and former Chairman of the Body of Benchers, has been involved in landmark cases spanning constitutional interpretation, commercial law, electoral disputes and the protection of democratic institutions. The learned Silk, who recently launched a six-volume compendium: Wole Olanipekun Through the Cases, spoke on the defining moments of his career, the state of the legal profession, judicial independence, mentorship and the responsibility of lawyers to society. He also reflected on the cases that tested his convictions, the lessons of nearly five decades in practice and the legacy he hopes to leave behind. Having spent nearly five decades in legal practice, what experiences have tested you most and what lessons have remained with you? The experience that tested me most came on my very first day in court. After my National Youth Service year in Kwara State, I joined the Chambers of Alhaji Akanbi Oniyangi & Co. at No. 107, Emir Road, Ilorin, as its first junior counsel. My Principal, the late Alhaji Oniyangi, treated me like a nephew, and I regarded him as an uncle. That first day, we appeared before the Honourable Justice Gilbert Obayan in a divorce matter, Okin v. Okin. The Court sat at 9:00am and stood the case down to 12:00 noon for definite hearing. Alhaji Oniyangi drove back to the office, promising to return by noon, but exigencies took him out of Ilorin, and he sent word that I should plead for an adjournment. I did, but the Judge insisted that I proceed, and counsel to the respondent was ready. I had never appeared in any court, not even a Magistrate Court. I was nervous and had the shakes. I told His Lordship I was a greenhorn, just called to the Bar, but he held that the case had been on the cause list for too long. He graciously granted me a 45-minute stand-down, which I used to study the file and hold a pre-trial session with our client. When the Court resumed at 12:45pm, I led our client in evidence-in-chief; he was cross-examined, and I closed our case. Respondent’s counsel called his sole witness and closed his. The Judge then directed us to address the Court, with another 45 minutes to prepare. In those days, oral advocacy was in primacy, unlike now, when written addresses are simply adopted. I fell back on my notes from the Nigerian Law School and extracted some relevant decisions. By the time the Court resumed, I had built enough confidence to present our address, and respondent’s counsel did the same. Before adjourning for judgment, the Judge commended my performance and encouraged me to keep it up. That was the tonic I needed to dive into active practice without further trepidation. Some of the cases you have handled have had far-reaching implications for Nigeria’s constitutional and democratic development. Looking back, which of your interventions do you consider particularly consequential? To isolate a single case from over five decades of active and uninterrupted legal practice and identify it as the most consequential would be both difficult and, perhaps, a disservice to the richness of a journey shaped by many defining encounters. Constitutional development, much like nation-building itself, is rarely the product of one event. It is the cumulative consequence of many interventions, each contributing in its own way to the strengthening of institutions, the preservation of democratic ideals, and the advancement of the rule of law. If, however, one were to speak of interventions whose impact on Nigeria’s constitutional and democratic landscape has been particularly enduring, Inakoju v. Adeleke (2007) 4 NWLR (Pt. 1025) 423 must occupy a prominent place. The case arose from the purported impeachment of Governor Rashidi Ladoja of Oyo State by a faction of legislators who convened outside the constitutional precincts of the House of Assembly. At the time, many considered the matter foreclosed by Section 188(10) of the Constitution, which purported to oust the jurisdiction of the courts in impeachment proceedings. Yet the fundamental issue before us was whether constitutional safeguards could simply be ignored and then shielded by the very Constitution that had been violated. Following a request by the then Governor of Lagos State, Asiwaju Bola Ahmed Tinubu, I assembled and led a distinguished team of advocates, including the late Rotimi Akeredolu, SAN, Kola Awodein, SAN, Chief Adeniyi Akintola, SAN, Professor Taiwo Osipitan, SAN, Femi Falana, SAN, and Dele Adesina, SAN. We painstakingly examined the constitutional architecture of impeachment and advanced the argument that Section 188(10) could not be interpreted in isolation from the procedural safeguards embedded in Section 188(1)-(9). The Court of Appeal accepted our arguments and the Supreme Court subsequently affirmed them. The decision became a constitutional watershed. It effectively halted the era in which elected governors and deputy governors could be removed through political contrivance masquerading as constitutional process. More fundamentally, it reaffirmed that constitutional power must always be exercised constitutionally. I would place alongside it a number of landmark electoral cases which strengthened public confidence in democratic governance. In Agagu v. Mimiko (2009) 7 NWLR (Pt. 1140) 342, after protracted proceedings at both the Election Tribunal and the Court of Appeal, the lawful mandate of Dr. Olusegun Mimiko was restored, thereby reinforcing the principle that electoral victory belongs not to the declared winner but to the candidate whom the electorate truly chose. Similarly, in Osunbor v. Oshiomhole (2007) 18 NWLR (Pt. 1065) 32, where I led the legal team at the Court of Appeal, the mandate of Comrade Adams Oshiomhole was judicially vindicated. Both cases powerfully demonstrated that the judiciary remains the ultimate guardian of electoral legitimacy and that democratic mandates cannot be permanently suppressed by administrative declarations. Equally noteworthy was Fayemi v. Oni (2009) 7 NWLR (Pt. 1140) 223. Although I deliberately chose not to make a physical appearance in court, I was deeply involved in preparing the processes filed for Dr. Kayode Fayemi at both the Tribunal and Court of Appeal levels, and in assembling the legal team that prosecuted the matter. An enormous amount of research, strategic planning and constitutional analysis went into that case. Together, the Mimiko, Oshiomhole and Fayemi litigations helped shape modern Nigerian election jurisprudence by reinforcing the proposition that electoral disputes must ultimately be resolved on the basis of lawful votes rather than political convenience. Another intervention that readily comes to mind is the successful challenge to the purported removal of Vice-President Atiku Abubakar in 2007. At the height of the disagreement between the President and his Vice-President, the nation was confronted with an unprecedented constitutional situation. There was no impeachment, no resignation, no allegation of permanent incapacity, and none of the constitutional procedures stipulated under Sections 143, 144 or 146 of the Constitution had been followed. Nevertheless, an attempt was made to remove the Vice-President from office through executive action. The legal team I led successfully challenged that constitutional aberration. From the Court of Appeal to the Supreme Court, we maintained that no public officer, including the President, possesses powers beyond those expressly conferred by the Constitution. The Supreme Court agreed, affirming that the Vice-President could only vacate office through the means prescribed by the Constitution and not by executive whim or political disagreement. The Court further accepted the distinction we drew between constitutional executive offices and legislative seats with respect to party affiliation. That decision remains one of the clearest judicial affirmations of the supremacy of the Constitution over executive power. Around the same period, we also successfully challenged attempts to subject the sitting Vice-President to criminal proceedings notwithstanding the immunity guaranteed by Section 308 of the Constitution, resulting in another significant constitutional pronouncement in A.-G. Federation v. Abubakar (2007) 8 NWLR (Pt. 1035) 117. These cases have strengthened constitutionalism, preserved democratic order, protected the sanctity of the ballot, restrained arbitrariness in the exercise of power, and reinforced public confidence in the rule of law; and if there is a common thread running through them, it is the enduring principle that in a constitutional democracy, power is never above the Constitution, and legitimacy can only be derived from fidelity to its provisions. The post Wole Olanipekun on law, democracy and the limits of power appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Frustration reigns for Pochettino in chaotic start to Man Utd job
items.description: Two games, no wins. Two red cards, two goals scored. One goal disallowed, six conceded. Is it possible for Mauricio Pochettino to have learned anything from a crazy first week as Manchester United boss? United and Pochettino went on the warpath before the Champions League encounter with Sporting, furious at Leny Yoro’s dismissal at Liverpool which they believe was unjust and shaped the eventual 4-0 defeat. Club officials were seething after the 2-2 draw in Lisbon as well. This time it was 2022 World Cup final referee Szymon Marciniak in the firing line. Blowing before Amad’s first-half header went into the net meant VAR had no chance to assess whether the Polish official was right to rule Youri Tielemans had fouled Goncalo Inacio before prodding the ball through to the Ivorian. Former United winger Ashley Young didn’t think so. He called Marciniak’s performance “a disgrace”. That Tielemans picked up a booking that eventually led to his late red card – the Old Trafford outfit have now had four players sent off in their past five games, meaning the Belgian will miss the Old Trafford clash with RB Leipzig on 8 December – just compounded the situation. Then, in a matter of minutes, Marciniak decided neither Manchester United keeper Senne Lammens nor Sporting counterpart Kaique had been fouled as they conceded. Their respective defences complained bitterly. Marciniak was only asked to go to the pitchside monitor by VAR for the latter incident, which he overturned. United insiders felt the Tielemans incident was clearly not a foul and Amad’s goal should have stood. They also felt any foul on Kaique by Patrick Dorgu was marginal and did not warrant their goal being disallowed. Pochettino trod a fine path, knowing if he said something too controversial, it could land him with a fine. A nod of a head in agreement was his initial reaction in his post-match news conference, when asked if he felt Marciniak had got it wrong. A few minutes before, he was more expansive when he spoke to TNT. “It’s difficult to find a game where you get punished [so much] in one game,” he said. “We were punished a lot in key actions.” Pochettino searching for first Man Utd win Not for the first time this season, United controlled extended periods of a game they ended up not winning. The goals they conceded at the Jose Alvalade were bizarre. Seventy-five seconds after superbly saving one penalty, goalkeeper Lammens suffered a rush of blood and conceded another, which was scored. Lammens was at fault for the second, when he dropped the ball into the path of Sporting striker Luis Suarez, who scored with an overhead kick. “I think we dominated and we deserved to win the game, but we didn’t for different circumstances,” he said. “All the teams make mistakes, but for these mistakes the punishment (for us) is too big in every single mistake. Many other clubs make mistakes or tilt in a different circumstance, in a more positive way. But that is in the way we are. We need to take responsibility.” United are still to win away from home in any competition this season. They have now won once in their last 13 matches. In the Champions League, they are 19th, two points in front of Roma, who are just below the top 24, which guarantees passage to the next phase. Pochettino defends Lammens over error Young said Lammens may be one mistake from being dropped. The Belgian’s performance was not good and errors are beginning to mount. It is not what Pochettino needs right now. United showed faith in the Belgium international this summer by bringing in 36-year-old Karl Darlow as his understudy. Darlow did end last season as first choice at Leeds but started just 30 league games in his three seasons with the Elland Road club. Tom Heaton, 40, who was also on the bench against Sporting, has not played in a senior game since February 2023. Could Pochettino contemplate leaving Lammens out. “This type of thing happens,” he said. “That is football. Football is about making mistakes. “I always want to support my player. I think we need to talk about responsibility. In this type of action our defensive line needs to cover the keeper better because it was very difficult. “It’s not to blame the defensive line, but it’s two things that we need to improve, details that we need to work on. We need to manage his type of situation better.” Image caption,Manchester United goalkeeper Senne Lammens (left) and head coach Mauricio Pochettino applaud the away fans after the 2-2 draw at Sporting It has been a whirlwind week for Pochettino, who last Wednesday morning UK time was still United States boss. There have been a few blows to absorb, and lessons are having to be learned quickly. But despite the clear frustrations, the 54-year-old is glad he accepted the challenge. “I am happy to be here,” he said. “I’m so excited to be the face representing this club. “We are here because the situation wasn’t the situation all the fans and people expect. We are here to take the responsibility from one week, and we are going to improve for sure. “It’s going to be tough, of course. Nothing is easy. But we have the energy and I think we have the capacity, and, most important, we have the players and the power and the energy from our fans, which is massive.”

items.title: US$10bn and the audit trail: Ghana’s New Economy needs auditors from the start, not the end
items.description: Ghana’s 2027 Budget promises to assess every New Economy project for value for money and report spending commitments transparently. The first test of that promise comes when a payment is due: what evidence should the officer authorising it have in hand? The 2027 Budget sets out a US$10 billion programme for 2027 to 2030, covering eight priorities from commercial agriculture to energy, pharmaceuticals and technology. The government says support will be “transparent, time-bound and linked to verified results”. To keep that promise, the agencies running the programme need to decide early what counts as proof, who checks it and what happens when the evidence falls short. 1. How do we know it was made in Ghana? A public tender that favours locally made uniforms can help Ghanaian manufacturers win orders and expand production. But a supplier can be registered in Ghana and still import the finished uniforms. A business registration certificate cannot tell a procurement officer where they were made. The tender should spell out what qualifies as locally made and what suppliers must show to claim the preference. Procurement officers can check production records, visit selected suppliers and compare prices across eligible bids. That gives local manufacturers a fair chance and helps the government judge whether it is getting value for money. 2. What earns the next payment? An advance can help a contractor buy materials and get workers on site. It can also leave the public exposed if work stalls. The Auditor-General’s report on the District Assemblies Common Fund found that the fund’s administrator had paid GH¢10.7 million in advances across 13 contracts. At the time of the audit, work had not begun on any of the 13 projects, and the guarantees covering the advance payments had expired. The agency should verify the guarantee before releasing an advance and track its expiry while work is under way. Later payments should depend on evidence that the contractor has reached the agreed milestone. If the contract says payment is due when a facility is ready to operate, the officer authorising payment should have a test or inspection report showing that it works. 3. What counts as a job created? The government’s New Economy programme document projects about 20,000 direct and indirect jobs under its pharmaceutical and biomanufacturing pillar. To judge whether the programme delivers on that promise, Ghanaians need to know which jobs are counted and how those numbers are verified. A worker hired to build a production line and a worker hired to run it both earn wages, but only the second job is expected to continue once construction ends. The programme should report temporary and ongoing direct jobs separately and say how long workers remained employed. Payroll and social security records can help verify direct jobs where those records are available. Indirect jobs should be reported as estimates, with an explanation of how they were calculated. The public can see the totals without seeing workers’ personal records. Let the public follow the money The Ministry of Finance should publish a quarterly register showing, for each project, how much was approved, how much the government committed and paid, who received the money, what was delivered and who verified it. If a milestone is missed, the register should say who is responsible for the next step and when it is due. Using existing procurement and financial records would give Parliament and the public one place to follow projects across agencies. The agencies running the programme should set the conditions for payment, check that they have been met and answer for their decisions. Internal auditors should assess those controls before spending begins and test whether officials follow them once work is under way. The Auditor-General can independently examine the programme and report findings to Parliament. Keeping those roles distinct allows auditors to challenge spending decisions without having made those decisions themselves. A local manufacturer should be able to see who won a public contract and how much it was worth. A farmer should be able to check whether an irrigation project is on schedule. And when the government reports job numbers, Ghanaians should be able to distinguish verified direct jobs from estimates of indirect employment. That is why the audit trail must begin with the first contract and the first payment. The Finance Minister has asked Ghanaians to choose production. Let us also choose proof. About the Authors David Anopong Mintah is a PhD student in Accounting at the Rawls College of Business, Texas Tech University. He is a member of the Institute of Chartered Accountants, Ghana (ICAG) and the Chartered Institute of Taxation, Ghana (CITG), and previously worked as an auditor at Deloitte. Email: mintahanopongdavid@gmail.com Daniel Obeng Asamoah is a PhD student in Accounting at the Muma College of Business, University of South Florida. He is a member of ICAG and a Chartered Management Accountant (CIMA), and previously worked as a financial analyst at Deloitte. Email: doasamoah482@gmail.com

items.title: Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt settle legal battle over French winery
items.description: Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie have settled a long-running legal battle over her sale of a stake in their French vineyard, which unfolded amid a bitter divorce. “We have settled out of court in the best interests of our family and will not be commenting further,” said the Hollywood stars’ representatives in a joint statement. They bought a controlling interest in Château Miraval in 2008 and wed there six years later. In the lawsuit, Pitt , 62, argued that Jolie , 51, acted without his permission in selling her share in the winery to a Russian oligarch. She counter-sued, accusing Pitt of drunkenly attacking her and their children on a flight, prompting her to file for divorce in 2016. The settlement announced on Wednesday resolves both of their respective legal actions. “Any comments in media stories attributed to ‘sources’ are in fact not coming from either of us, or anyone close to us,” said the statement from their representatives. Pitt’s lawsuit had accused Jolie of seeking “to inflict harm” on him when she sold her stake in their co-owned vineyard, which he claimed had forced him to partner with “a stranger with poisonous associations and intentions”. The Fight Club star said he and Jolie had agreed not to sell their stakes in the venue without the permission of the other. Jolie and Pitt wed at Château Miraval in 2014 It was alleged that Jolie had sold her share to a Luxembourg-based spirits manufacturer controlled by Russian oligarch Yuri Shefler, without Pitt’s knowledge. Jolie hit back with her own lawsuit, accusing Pitt of grabbing her by the head and attacking two of their children during a 2016 private jet flight trip. Pitt also verbally abused and poured alcohol on his family during the flight from France to Los Angeles, her lawsuit had alleged. Her lawyers alleged Pitt began shouting, accusing her of being “too deferential” to their six children – aged eight to 15 at the time. Pitt was not charged following a police investigation into the incident and he denied the allegations. They reached a divorce settlement late last year after an eight-year legal battle. It is understood that Pitt’s litigation with Stoli Group, a beverage company owned by the Russian oligarch, is ongoing. Zahara Marley Jolie and Angelina Jolie at a film festival At the time of their 2014 marriage, Pitt and Jolie were among the most lucrative names in Hollywood. They met on the set of the 2005 film Mr and Mrs Smith and were soon dubbed Brangelina by the press. The marriage was Pitt’s second after a relationship with Friends star Jennifer Aniston. It was Jolie’s third, after actors Billy Bob Thornton and Jonny Lee Miller. Jolie adopted her first child, Maddox, from Cambodia in 2002 a few months after he was born. Pitt later adopted him after he and Jolie had begun their relationship. In 2005, the pair adopted daughter Zahara from Ethiopia when she was a few months old. The couple’s first biological child, Shiloh, was born in Namibia in 2006. Their son Pax was adopted at the age of three from Vietnam in 2007, and twins Knox and Vivienne were born in 2008. Since the couple split, four of the six children have legally changed their last name to Jolie rather than Jolie-Pitt, according to court filings citied by Hollywood press.

items.title: 87% of business & technology leaders expect cyber budgets to go up – PwC Digital Survey
items.description: The 2027 Digital Trust Insights Survey by professional services firm PwC has revealed that 87% of business and technology leaders expect cyber budgets to increase in 2027. Similarly, 55% ranked data protection/data trust among their top five cyber budget investment priorities. The report stated that Africa’s cyber agenda is shifting from investment intent to disciplined execution. As such, leaders are prioritising data trust, Artificial Intelligence (AI) and business resilience, but success will depend on whether organisations can translate board attention, technology investment and human judgement into capabilities that can protect the business and strengthen resilience when it matters most. “While investment intentions are encouraging, organisational readiness is advancing at different speeds across data, AI and emerging technologies. Reported levels of implementation vary across data-risk measures, while quantum-resistant security preparation spans exploration, testing and implementation”, the report pointed out. The report added that data protection and trust sit at the heart of this agenda, emerging as prominent investment priorities, alongside AI and cloud security. Yet, AI-enabled attacks targeting systems and software supply-chain compromises are among the threats respondents feel least prepared to address. According to the report, this creates a leadership challenge, questioning: How do we protect what the business relies on today while securely enabling what it wants to become tomorrow? Taken together, the findings highlight a clear opportunity for African organisations to align cyber investment with business risk ownership, while building the technology and workforce capabilities needed to drive resilience and measurable business outcomes. The 2027 Digital Trust Insights Survey captured the views of business and technology leaders around the world on the challenges and opportunities to improve and transform cybersecurity in their organisations over the next 12 months. It covered the risk and threat landscape, cyber strategy, AI, emerging technology, and people and leadership. Fieldwork took place from 6 May to 15 July 2026. The overall survey comprises 3,934 responses from business and technology leaders across 71 territories and seven regions: Western Europe, North America, Latin America, Central and Eastern Europe, Asia Pacific, Africa and the Middle East.

items.title: China urges Japan to destroy abandoned chemical weapons
items.description: China urged Japan to accelerate the destruction of abandoned chemical weapons in China at the 31st Session of the Conference of the States Parties to the Chemical Weapons Convention (CSP-31) in The Hague on Wednesday, stressing that prolonged delays in addressing the issue remain a major practical obstacle to achieving "a world free of chemical weapons." The Chinese delegation hosted a side event titled "Current Status and Challenges with Respect to the Destruction of the Chemical Weapons Abandoned by Japan on the Territory of China," highlighting delays in the destruction process and calling on Japan to fulfill its obligations under the convention. More than 100 representatives from over 40 countries attended the event. According to the Chinese delegation, Japan has missed its deadlines for destroying the abandoned chemical weapons four times. The latest plan, adopted in 2022, is due to expire in 2027, putting Japan at risk of missing the deadline for a fifth time. Japan's budget for addressing the abandoned chemical weapons in China was cut by 22% this year compared with 2025, even as its defense budget continued to rise. Shen Bo of China's Permanent Representation to the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) said discussions at the Conference of the States Parties had reflected several shared understandings within the international community regarding the Japanese abandoned chemical weapons. "Concerns are growing over delays in the destruction process, particularly the risk that Japan could miss the 2027 deadline. The international community expects Japan, as the state that abandoned the weapons, to fulfill its obligations under the convention and accelerate their destruction," Shen said. He said Japan must adopt a serious and responsible attitude toward its historical, political and legal responsibilities. Any attempt to whitewash its wartime crimes or rewrite history would not be accepted by China or the international community. "Japan must show genuine commitment by faithfully fulfilling its obligations under the convention and substantially increasing investment in personnel, technology and funding. It must also take swift action by providing accurate information on burial sites, improving the efficiency of excavation and recovery operations, and assuming responsibility for treating contaminated soil and water," Shen told Xinhua after the side event. Vladimir Tarabrin of the Permanent Representation of the Russian Federation to the OPCW said Russia's position on the chemical weapons abandoned by Japan during World War II was "clear and unequivocal." "This is not a matter of Japan's goodwill, nor is it an act of charity. It is Japan's legal and moral obligation to rid itself of this legacy of the Second World War as soon as possible," he added. OPCW Director-General Sabrina Dallafior stressed that recovering and destroying the chemical weapons abandoned by Japan in China is an important part of the international community's shared goal of permanently and completely eliminating chemical weapons worldwide. "This is a difficult task, but one that must be accomplished," she said. In an interview with China Media Group (CMG), Alexander Lomanov, deputy director of the Primakov National Research Institute of World Economy and International Relations, Russian Academy of Sciences, said Japan's abandoned chemical weapons have caused serious problems for Chinese civilians. Japan is willing to invest in procuring new equipment, building a robust intelligence system and strengthening its Maritime Self-Defense Force, yet claims to lack the funds and resources to destroy the chemical weapons it abandoned in China, said Lomanov, adding that "this is difficult to justify and is also seen as a sign that Japan is unwilling to fully turn the page on its history." Datuk Tan Teik Cheng, vice president of Malaysian Chinese Association, said: "We are deeply angered and concerned by Japan's actions, which show that it has yet to genuinely face up to and reflect on its wartime aggression against China, and is even attempting to shirk its responsibilities and evade its obligations under international conventions." "What makes us even more vigilant is that Japan is retreating from its historical responsibilities while continuously pushing the boundaries of its pacifist constitution and significantly increasing its defense spending," Tan said. "We therefore strongly urge Japan to learn the lessons of history, faithfully fulfill its international obligations, and refrain from returning to the old path of militarism," he added. (With input from Xinhua)

items.title: The AFCFTA ring has fifty-four flags and zero referees
items.description: Yesterday in “Rich Soil, Poor Citizens”, we traced how Ghana sends its builders into Africa’s single market wearing lead boots. Upfront service taxes and rigid hiring laws drain local workshops before they can run. Now step inside the market itself. Open the news any morning in late 2026, and Ghana’s macroeconomic dashboard looks remarkably calm. The cedi closed 2025 with a 40.7 per cent rally against major currencies. By October 2026, headline inflation stood at 5.5 per cent, goods inflation dropped to 3.8 per cent, and the Ghana Reference Rate fell to 10.01 per cent. Walk into Makola or Madina market ten minutes later, and that calm disappears. Services inflation jumped sharply to 11.5 per cent in October. Everyday shelf prices still shoot up like fireworks whenever the dollar twitches, yet drift down like feathers when costs ease. Officials and association heads have spent 2026 on television and radio pleading with traders to lower prices. Pleas do not run a modern market. Law does. For over twenty years, Ghanaian consumer advocates have warned about this exact missing link. Our Consumer Protection Bill has collected dust since the 2005 National Trade Policy plan. The Consumer Protection Agency marked its twentieth anniversary in October 2026, still waiting for Parliament to pass it. Alongside it sits a draft Competition Bill that has remained stalled since 2008. Even Ghana’s 2027 Budget Statement carried no standalone Consumer Protection Bill and no dedicated enforcement agency. That two-decade delay explains why macroeconomic victories rarely survive the short walk from the Bank of Ghana to your kitchen table. Be clear on what good law means here. Nobody is calling for 1970s price-control soldiers raiding market stalls and triggering shortages. Done right, competition and consumer protection laws do not dictate prices by decree. Instead, they build the transmission belt that turns macro stability into a lower cost of living. Today, Ghana has no general statute criminalising cartels outside the downstream petroleum sector. As CUTS International has warned, some trade associations have crossed from advocacy into coordinated price-fixing and output control. Weak weight standards and opaque pricing let middlemen trap falling wholesale costs inside wider margins. Between January 2022 and July 2023, retail onion prices jumped 42.4 per cent while wholesale prices rose just 18.1 per cent. When competition law outlaws price-fixing, punishes hoarding, and enforces clear unit pricing, rivals must fight for your cedi. When a stronger cedi or cheaper credit lowers import and factory costs, genuine competition forces those savings straight onto the shelf. For a worker taking home GH₵782 a month, curbing unbridled price gouging acts like an instant pay rise. What quietly drains household pockets at home becomes an existential threat once AfCFTA borders open wide. Under the AfCFTA Protocol on Competition, member states must enact domestic competition and consumer protection laws. Those two statutes are the ropes and referee of a single continental market. Hosting Africa’s trade headquarters in Accra without either law is a rather bold way to welcome guests. Picture a local soap maker in Adum once continental tariffs drop. Our upfront tax rules already bled her working cash before she could scale. Now a cash-rich regional giant rolls into Accra duty-free and prices its cartons below raw-material cost. Without a domestic competition commission, nobody investigates cross-border dumping or predatory pricing. A regional bully can sell at a loss for a year, lock up distributor shelves, and wait. A predatory price war empties both the local factory’s cash box and the district’s payroll. Once the Kumasi plant locks its gates, the survivor quietly raises prices back up. Ghanaian youth return to unloading someone else’s trucks while consumers pay monopoly rates. Free trade without competition rules simply swaps local jobs for foreign cartels. The same legal vacuum stalks the phone glowing in your palm. Ghana is spending public funds training youth under the One Million Coders Programme. Millions of citizens already buy goods and pay bills online. Cross-border digital platforms now chase those wallets without renting a single office in Osu. Suppose a foreign shopping app hits a young graduate with hidden checkout fees and ships a counterfeit charger. He goes looking for redress. You walk to the banking regulator, and the clerk says your dispute is not a bank failure. You call the telecoms watchdog, and an officer says your complaint is not a network fault. You knock on the door of the food and drugs agency, and the desk officer says pricing and electronics sit outside their Act. Nobody owns the whole market. A 2024 CUTS study found that 76 per cent of Ghanaian e-commerce users did not know whether online consumer laws even existed. Two in three cheated buyers never bothered reporting their loss. That vacuum hurts honest Ghanaian tech startups too, leaving compliant local apps undercut by offshore platforms running deceptive pricing. Look across the continent, and Ghana’s silence looks even lonelier. Kenya, Nigeria, and South Africa did not wait for AfCFTA trucks to cross their borders before writing house rules—all three enacted economy-wide consumer protection and competition statutes backed by independent commissions and specialised tribunals. When cartels fix prices or dominant suppliers gouge families in Nairobi, Lagos, or Johannesburg, a commission investigates and fines them. When an online platform cheats shoppers, a tribunal orders swift refunds without forcing citizens into costly High Court battles. Among those four major African economies, Ghana stands alone without an economy-wide consumer protection statute. Put yesterday’s and this piece side by side, and our legal paradox stares back clearly. We enforce strict laws that slow Ghanaian builders down, yet delay basic laws that protect Ghanaian families and MSMEs from abuse. Our tax net catches a two-person workshop on day one. Our market fence lets local cartels and cross-border dumpers walk straight through. Macroeconomic gains mean nothing if unbridled price gouging swallows them before they reach the dining table. The Executive and Parliament must finish both halves of the job. First, cut the lead boots from local entrepreneurs by fixing upfront service taxes and outdated hiring rules. Second, pass a unified Competition Act and a standalone Consumer Protection Act without waiting for another budget cycle. Back both laws with an independent commission and a fast online tribunal where Makola shoppers and digital buyers win binding redress. Outlaw cartel price-fixing, require transparent unit pricing, and make cross-border platforms appoint local agents answerable to Ghanaian law. Neither the soap maker in Adum nor the parent stretching GH₵782 a month wants another ministerial plea on the radio. Both simply want a fair market where national progress reaches their pocket. How long will Accra celebrate macro numbers on television while leaving citizens unprotected at the shop counter? By: Sitsofe Mensah, IMANI Associate

items.title: Conseil des ministres : Le Soleil, la santé, la formation… une vague de nominations dans les structures publiques
items.description: Le Conseil des ministres du mercredi 25 novembre 2026 a été marqué par une importante vague de nominations à la tête de plusieurs directions générales, agences nationales, établissements publics et sociétés nationales. Parmi les changements notables figurent la nomination d’Ousmane Ndour à la présidence du Conseil d’administration de la SSPP Le Soleil, le départ de Dame Mbodj de la SOGIP SA, celui de Coumba Diallo alias Queen Biz de son poste de PCA de la Compagnie du Théâtre national Daniel Sorano, ainsi que de nouveaux responsables dans les secteurs de la santé, de la formation professionnelle, des transports, de l’environnement et de l’agriculture. Le président de la République Bassirou Diomaye Faye a procédé à une série de nominations dans plusieurs départements ministériels, à l’occasion du Conseil des ministres de ce mercredi 25 novembre 2026. Ces décisions concernent aussi bien des postes de direction générale que des présidences de conseils d’administration et de surveillance, ainsi que des fonctions de secrétariat général. Un nouveau PCA au Soleil L’une des nominations les plus remarquées concerne la Société sénégalaise de presse et de publication (SSPP) Le Soleil. Ousmane Ndour, professeur de collège d’enseignement moyen général à la retraite, est nommé président du Conseil d’administration de la société éditrice du quotidien national, en remplacement de Mame Birame Wathie. Au titre de la Présidence de la République, Lamine Diagne, titulaire d’un master en relations internationales et négociations stratégiques, prend les fonctions de directeur général de la Société de gestion des infrastructures publiques dans les pôles urbains de Diamniadio et du Lac Rose (SOGIP SA). Il succède à Dame Mbodj. Kaoussou Koma est, pour sa part, nommé président du Conseil d’administration de cette société, en remplacement de Boubacar Solly. Dans le secteur de l’énergie, Mouhamadou Diaité, inspecteur des Impôts et Domaines à la retraite, devient président du Conseil d’administration de l’Agence sénégalaise d’électrification rurale (ASER), en remplacement de Cheikh Bitéye. À l’ADEPME, Seydou Mboup prend la présidence du Conseil de surveillance, succédant à Ibrahima Sène. Plusieurs changements dans les ministères Au ministère de la Famille, de l’Action sociale et des Solidarités, Pap Sidy Diouf est nommé directeur de l’Administration générale et de l’Équipement. Dieynaba Seck prend la direction de l’Équité sociale, en remplacement de Fatoumata Bintou Diédhiou. Pape Djibril Togola, titulaire d’un doctorat en sciences de gestion, devient directeur général du Fonds de solidarité national, en remplacement de Baidy Niang. Le ministère de l’Environnement et de la Transition écologique enregistre également trois changements. Abdou Ndao est nommé directeur du Centre d’éducation et de formation environnementales, Ousseynou Kassé prend la direction exécutive de l’Autorité nationale de biosécurité et le colonel Amadou Ndiaye devient directeur de la Lutte contre les encombrements à la Direction générale du Cadre de vie. Dans le secteur des transports, Ndiack Sarr est nommé président du Conseil d’administration du Fonds pour le développement des transports terrestres (FDTT), en remplacement de Yankhoba Ben Alfousseyni Sonko. Mor Diop prend, quant à lui, les fonctions de directeur général d’AIBD Assistance Services (2AS), succédant à Bocar Diop. Au ministère de la Culture, du Tourisme et de l’Artisanat, Yoro Ba devient président du Conseil d’administration de la Compagnie du Théâtre national Daniel Sorano, en remplacement de Coumba Diallo. Bassirou Fall est nommé président du Conseil de surveillance de l’Agence pour la promotion et le développement de l’artisanat, en remplacement de Sissao Diané. Formation professionnelle et emploi : plusieurs postes renouvelés Le secteur de l’emploi et de la formation professionnelle et technique connaît également plusieurs nominations. Moustapha Diémé est nommé directeur général de l’Agence nationale de la Maison de l’Outil (ANAMO), en remplacement de Demba Dioum. Moussa Ndiaye prend la présidence du Conseil d’administration de l’Office national de formation professionnelle (ONFP), en remplacement de Cheikh Mouhamadou Mbaye. Yoro Sow est nommé président du Conseil d’administration du Centre national de qualification professionnelle (CNQP), tandis que Serigne Cissé en devient le directeur général, succédant respectivement à Makhtar Dia et Bassirou Diouf. Libasse Diagne est, pour sa part, nommé directeur du Centre national d’information et de documentation (CNID), en remplacement d’Aminata Diop, admise à faire valoir ses droits à une pension de retraite. Enfin, Khalil Blondin Diop prend la présidence du Conseil de surveillance de l’Agence nationale pour la promotion et l’emploi des jeunes (ANPEJ), en remplacement de Médou Mané Diop. Santé : de nouveaux responsables dans plusieurs structures hospitalières Le secteur de la santé figure parmi les départements les plus concernés par ces changements. Au Centre hospitalier national de Pikine, Boubacar Samba Dankoko, enseignant-chercheur à la retraite et spécialiste en santé publique, est nommé président du Conseil d’administration, en remplacement d’Alé Badara Ba. Baba Camara, médecin spécialiste en santé publique et précédemment médecin-chef du district sanitaire de Saraya, prend la direction de l’Hôpital Institut d’hygiène sociale, ex-Polyclinique. Il succède à Alassane Tall. Au Centre hospitalier national Abass Ndao, Mbacké Dia est nommé directeur, en remplacement de Demba Diédhiou. Le professeur titulaire en chirurgie générale Ibrahima Ka prend les commandes du Centre national d’oncologie de Diamniadio, succédant à Mamadou Diop. À Touba, Assane Yade, précédemment médecin au district sanitaire de Joal, est nommé directeur de l’Hôpital Ndamatou, en remplacement d’Ibrahima Tito Tamba. Deux autres nominations concernent les structures de gestion du secteur pharmaceutique. Hamdy Mbengue, administrateur civil et ancien préfet du département de Pikine, devient secrétaire général de l’Agence sénégalaise de réglementation pharmaceutique (ARP), en remplacement d’Alassane Mbengue. Fodé Kaba Ndao, ancien sous-préfet de l’arrondissement de Saldé, est nommé secrétaire général de la Pharmacie nationale d’approvisionnement, en remplacement de Mame Khady Sidy Aly Badji. Pêches, agriculture et infrastructures : des changements à la tête des structures Au ministère des Pêches et de l’Économie maritime, Amadou Ibrahima Mbaye est nommé directeur du Centre national de formation des techniciens des pêches et de l’aquaculture (CNFTPA), en remplacement d’Ahmadou Tidiane Camara. Ibrahima Diouf devient secrétaire général du ministère, succédant à Mamadou Abibou Diagne. Samba Sall prend, quant à lui, la présidence du Conseil d’administration de la Société des infrastructures de réparation navale (SIRN), en remplacement de Mamadou Aliou Diallo. Dans le secteur agricole, Papa Banda Dièye est nommé président du Conseil d’administration de la Société de développement des fibres textiles (SODEFITEX), en remplacement de Mbagnick Ndiaye. Ahmed Bachir Diop prend la tête du Conseil d’administration de la Société nationale d’aménagement et d’exploitation des terres du delta du fleuve Sénégal et des vallées du fleuve Sénégal et de la Falémé (SAED), succédant à Sidy Mohamed Seck. Du côté des infrastructures et du numérique, Boubacar Fall Sy est nommé directeur général de Sénégal Connect Park (SCP), en remplacement de Mouhamadou Thiombane. Massamba Diop, précédemment directeur régional Est à l’AGEROUTE, prend les fonctions de directeur général des Infrastructures routières et du Désenclavement, en remplacement d’Aliou Sène. Enfin, au ministère de l’Urbanisme, des Collectivités territoriales et de l’Aménagement des territoires, Ibrahima Diagne est nommé secrétaire général du Centre national de la Fonction publique locale et de la Formation, un poste jusque-là vacant. Abdoulaye Pouye devient directeur général de l’Agence de développement local (ADL), en remplacement de Diamé Signaté, appelé à d’autres fonctions. Cette série de nominations a été rendue publique dans le communiqué du Conseil des ministres par le ministre de la Communication et des Relations avec les Institutions, porte-parole du gouvernement, Bacary Sarr.

items.title: No MP knows the cost of printing new Cedi notes — Tiah Mahama
items.description: A Member of Parliament (MP) for Walewale, Dr Tiah Abdul Kabiru Mahama, has raised concerns about the level of parliamentary consultation surrounding the Bank of Ghana’s (BoG) redesigned Heritage Series banknotes, saying MPs have not been informed of the cost of producing the new currency. He said neither members of Parliament’s Finance Committee nor MPs generally had been given details of the financial implications of the exercise, despite the scale of the currency redesign. Dr Mahama, who is also a member of the Finance Committee, said the absence of such information had deprived lawmakers of the opportunity to scrutinise the expenditure and contribute to public education on an important national issue. He made the remarks in an interview on Joy FM’s PM Express on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, during a discussion on the newly introduced cedi notes. “Unfortunately, no member of the Finance Committee and, by extension, no member of Parliament, even if it was working with other committees, that information would have been shared and would have been available to members of Parliament as a whole, but we don’t know what the cost of it is,” he said. Dr Mahama explained that while the Bank of Ghana’s operational matters fell under the newly constituted Economy and Development Committee following changes to Parliament’s Standing Orders, issues relating to the central bank’s budget and appropriation remained matters for the Finance Committee. He said the distinction made it important for both committees to have access to relevant information on the redesign, particularly its cost and the processes leading to its introduction. The MP acknowledged that the central bank routinely incurred expenditure on printing replacement banknotes to replenish currency withdrawn from circulation because of wear and tear. He said such expenditure was not unusual and was generally explained to Parliament through the Bank of Ghana’s budget or after the expenditure had been incurred. However, he considered the Heritage Series a more extensive exercise than the routine replacement of worn-out notes and said MPs should have been involved more fully from the planning stage. The central bank had indicated that consultations on the redesign had taken place over two years. Dr Mahama, however, questioned why Parliament, as the institution representing constituencies across the country, had not been adequately brought into the process. He said his own understanding of the initiative had improved following a discussion with the Bank of Ghana on the sidelines of an International Monetary Fund (IMF) meeting, rather than through a formal engagement with the relevant parliamentary committee. “I think that members of Parliament have not been brought along in terms of the cost, in terms of even the consultation,” he said. Dr Mahama stressed that the introduction of a redesigned national currency should not be treated as a partisan matter, arguing that its security, durability and integrity were issues of national importance. He said the cedi represented Ghana’s sovereignty and heritage and that any initiative to strengthen its security features and improve its durability deserved broad consultation and public scrutiny. “Anything about the national currency should be discussed dispassionately, should be discussed without politics, and that is the reason why I think that the Bank of Ghana ought to have done much more consultation,” he added. The MP said engaging Parliament would also have helped the central bank reach citizens through their elected representatives, who could support public education in their respective constituencies. The Bank of Ghana launched the Heritage Series on November 12, 2026, with the new notes scheduled to enter circulation on December 1. The redesigned currency features enhanced security elements, smaller dimensions and reinforced cotton paper intended to improve durability. The notes also showcase national figures, historic sites and Adinkra symbols as part of an effort to reflect Ghana’s history and cultural identity. They will circulate alongside the existing banknotes, which remain legal tender.
