items.title: Semaine du numérique 2026 : L'open source, l'IA, les langues nationales et l'accompagnement des start-up au cœur d'un panel
items.description: La 21e édition de la Semaine du numérique se poursuit ce mercredi 25 novembre 2026 au Parc d'exposition du Salon international de l'artisanat de Ouagadougou (SIAO). Pour cette deuxième journée, les échanges ont mis en lumière plusieurs défis liés à la souveraineté technologique du Burkina Faso tels que l'appropriation des technologies ouvertes, le développement de l'intelligence artificielle dans les langues nationales, la formation des compétences locales et le financement des entreprises numériques. Les échanges ont été modérés par Abdoul Kader Ky, directeur national de l'économie numérique du Niger. Pour Idriss Tinto, conseiller technique au ministère de la Transition digitale, des postes et des communications électroniques, l'open source est un levier de souveraineté. L'accès aux codes sources permet d'adapter les solutions existantes et réduit la dépendance aux grandes plateformes. Il met en garde contre les hausses de tarifs, les restrictions d'accès ou les interruptions de service décidées par les fournisseurs d'intelligence artificielle (IA), et plaide pour des compétences locales capables d'assurer la maintenance des outils. M. Tinto reconnaît les risques de l'ouverture, mais estime que la collaboration entre développeurs et utilisateurs aide à détecter les failles. Il invite les États à soutenir les communautés locales et voit aussi dans l'automatisation du code une occasion de faire évoluer les métiers plutôt qu'une simple menace pour l'emploi. Idriss Tinto, conseiller technique au ministère de la transition digitale, des postes et des communications électroniques. Faire parler l'IA en mooré La souveraineté passe aussi par les langues. Dr Rodrigue Kafando, enseignant-chercheur à l'Université virtuelle du Burkina Faso et chargé de recherche au Centre d'excellence en intelligence artificielle (CITADEL), a présenté des travaux sur quatre langues nationales : le mooré, le dioula, le fulfuldé et le gulmancema. Les équipes adaptent des modèles existants, notamment ceux de la famille NLLB de Meta, à partir de données collectées localement. Dr Rodrigue Kafando, enseignant-chercheur à l'Université virtuelle du Burkina Faso. Le principal obstacle reste selon lui la rareté de ressources variées. À l'en croire, les premiers essais en mooré se sont appuyés sur des textes bibliques et des documents relatifs aux droits humains, ce qui limite le vocabulaire maîtrisé par les modèles. M. Kafando préconise d'élargir la collecte aux traductions, aux transcriptions et aux enregistrements vocaux du quotidien, et de faire valider les évaluations par des locuteurs. Il cite l'outil ( https://lessentiel.bf ) qui rend l'actualité accessible en mooré par traduction automatique, et envisage des usages dans l'éducation, la santé et l'agriculture. Il appelle à mutualiser les données linguistiques entre chercheurs, développeurs, associations et institutions publiques. Vue partielle de participants du Mali et du Niger . Des compétences, mais aussi des clients Ounténi T. Cyril Ouoba, directeur général de RIGO, a identifié cinq domaines de formation prioritaires : le génie logiciel, les infrastructures, la cybersécurité, les données et l'IA, et la commercialisation. Sur ce dernier point, il juge l'écosystème insuffisant, car une innovation technique ne devient pas un produit viable sans compétences en marketing. Il demande que l'État et les grandes entreprises recourent davantage aux solutions locales, la commande publique pouvant constituer un débouché déterminant. Les innovations primées lors des hackathons devraient, selon lui, être déployées au-delà de la remise des prix. Ounténi T. Cyril Ouoba, directeur général de RIGO. Il recommande des formations courtes, de trois à six mois, pour les jeunes et les femmes déscolarisés, et l'introduction de l'algorithmique dès le collège. Il évoque aussi les commerçantes des marchés et des zones rurales, qui pourraient gérer stocks, ventes et comptabilité avec des applications vocales dans les langues nationales. M. Ouoba a également proposé de recenser les solutions numériques matures dans la comptabilité, la recherche, l'agriculture ou la santé. Les États de l'AES pourraient conduire ce travail et le présenter lors de la prochaine édition de la Semaine. Il suggère enfin un réseau de mentors, constitué avec les associations professionnelles des trois pays, pour accompagner les jeunes talents jusqu'à l'aboutissement de leurs projets. Il se dit réservé sur les aides financières immédiates. Des étudiants ont suivi avec attention les échanges qui ont duré plus de 2 heures de temps. Accompagner avant de financer Cette réserve a trouvé un écho dans l'intervention de Bourhanoud-Dine Sawadogo, chargé d'analyse économique et financière au Fonds burkinabè de développement économique et social (FBDES). Il a rappelé le bilan de l'Initiative Burkina Startups, lancée en 2017 avec une enveloppe annoncée de 10 milliards de francs CFA et l'ambition de faire naître 500 start-up. L'expérience a révélé des insuffisances dans la préparation et l'encadrement de certains porteurs de projets. Les échanges ont été modérés par Abdoul Kader Ky, directeur national de l'économie numérique du Niger. . Pour lui, il faut évaluer les besoins réels avant de mobiliser des fonds car certaines start-up manquent davantage de formation, d'équipements, de réseau ou d'appui technique que d'argent. Le parcours envisagé comprend la formation initiale, la sélection, la maturation des projets et l'accompagnement vers le marché, avec une attention particulière à l'existence d'une demande réelle. [ Cliquez ici pour lire l'intégralité ] Fredo Bassolé Lefaso.net

items.title: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor, sound of the 1980s, dies at 65
items.description: Andy Taylor, the former guitarist with new wave pop group Duran Duran, has died after a “long and courageous battle with prostate cancer”, the band and his family said on social media late on Wednesday. He was 65. “Andy passed away peacefully at home, surrounded by his family on Monday 23rd November,” they said in a joint statement. items.title: Awka City chosen for AfDB -funded Action Plan for Africa’s coordinated urban development
items.description: By Vincent Ujumadu Awka, the capital city of Anambra State, has been selected for the African Development Bank, AfDB, – funded action plan for coordinated urban development in Africa. Under the programme, government would provide the policy direction, regulatory clarity, and institutional leadership, while development partners would support the mobilisation of technical expertise and catalytic resources. Also, the private sector is expected to play a decisive role in financing and delivering viable infrastructure and urban projects, traditional institutions, community leaders, professional bodies and residents will remain vital in safeguarding public ownership and ensuring that development stays centred on the people in the new city. At the launch of the plan on Wednesday in Awka, the state governor, Professor Chukwuma Soludo said it is part of the strategic plan to create the envisioned Anambra mega city. Represented by his special Adviser on trade and commerce, Mr. Christian Udechukwu, the governor recalled that Awka is the only city chosen in Africa for the project, noting that it is because of the long term vision and the strategic implementation and the intentionality and purposeful focus of the administration. According to Udechukwu, it is the governor’s determination to transform Anambra State that drew the attention of the African Development Bank to the state. “The reforms they see here are of significance that it would serve to use Awka City as a model to prove the sustainability of the project and we are happy that this is happening under this administration”, he said. He said that a substantial amount of next year’s budget would be devoted to the development of the new Awka City, while other cities of Onitsha, Nnewi, and Ekwulobia would also undergo transformation, in addition to the new cities planned for the state. “When Awka 2.0 joins the planned industrial city, the proposed axis of prosperity would have been created. So Anambra is being positioned to become the economic hub of Nigeria and that is why the selection of Awka as a primary model sustainable city in Africa is important to us as a government. We should therefore not waste more time to move into the project preparatory stage”, Udechukwu said. Speaking at the launch, the Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Awka Capital Territory Development Authority, ACTDA, Dr Osita Onuko said the coordinated development framework is aimed at addressing the growing infrastructure and environmental challenges confronting Awka and guiding the capital city’s expansion towards a more liveable and inclusive future. The ACTDA boss said the action plan should be viewed not merely as a technical document, but as a shared commitment to building a productive, resilient and inclusive capital city for future generations He said: “This ambition aligns directly with the vision of His Excellency, Governor Chukwuma Soludo, to transform Anambra into a liveable and prosperous smart megacity by 2050. Achieving that vision requires clear urban direction, sustained investment, and strong institutions capable of translating bold aspirations into tangible outcomes. “Like many rapidly growing African cities, Awka is experiencing mounting pressure on its urban infrastructure, public services, and environment. The steady expansion of our built environment, rising demand for housing and utilities, traffic congestion, flooding, and gully erosion all highlight the urgent need for a more integrated approach to urban management. “These challenges are deeply interconnected. Addressing them effectively means that decisions around land use, mobility, housing, utilities, environmental protection, and economic development must be considered together within one coherent framework. Without this alignment, interventions risk becoming fragmented, resources are inefficiently deployed, and opportunities for lasting impact are lost. “The Awka City Action Plan provides that common framework. It establishes a shared direction for our capital’s growth, identifies clear priority areas for intervention, and creates a practical structure to align government spending, private sector investment, and development partner support. “With the document now complete, our immediate focus turns to translating these priorities into bankable, well-prepared projects that can attract financing and deliver lasting value. For ACTDA, this means providing strong institutional leadership and coordination—working hand-in-hand with relevant ministries, departments, and agencies to ensure this plan actively guides our regulatory decisions and investment discussions. We are committed to accountability, continuity, and measurable results so that this becomes a living framework rather than a document left on a shelf.” The post Awka City chosen for AfDB -funded Action Plan for Africa’s coordinated urban development appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Gaoua : Convaincu que sa cousine l’avait ensorcelé, il la tue à coups de machette et risque la prison à vie
items.description: Le 30 juillet 2024, dans un village de Malba, une affaire de meurtre impliquant deux membres d’une même famille a été enregistrée par le commissariat de police de Nako. À l’origine du drame, des soupçons de sorcellerie nourris par un homme à l’encontre de sa cousine. À la barre au Tribunal de Grande Instance de Gaoua ce mardi 24 novembre 2026, S. D. a reconnu avoir mortellement agressé cette dernière à coups de machette. Au regard des circonstances des faits, le procureur du Faso a requis la réclusion criminelle à perpétuité. Les faits remontent au 30 juillet 2024. Ce jour-là, S. D., muni d’une machette, se rend au domicile de sa cousine dans le but de l’interroger sur des pratiques de sorcellerie qu’il lui attribue. Ne l’ayant pas trouvée sur place, il poursuit ses recherches jusqu’au champ où elle travaillait. Après les salutations d’usage, il lui demande de le délivrer de ce qu’il considère comme un envoûtement. Face au silence de sa cousine, il passe à l’acte. Selon ses propres déclarations à la barre, il lui porte un premier coup de machette au cou, suivi d’un deuxième, puis d’un troisième. La victime s’effondre. Des soupçons de sorcellerie à l’origine du drame Pour expliquer son geste, S. D. évoque des problèmes de santé qu’il aurait commencé à ressentir après des échanges avec la victime à des funérailles. Il affirme avoir souffert, pendant environ un mois, de divers maux, notamment des douleurs au ventre, à la tête et au dos. Des manifestations qu’il attribue aux pratiques mystiques de sa cousine. Il explique également avoir prié dans une église pendant quelques jours. Mais, loin de dissiper ses inquiétudes, ces prières auraient renforcé ses soupçons à l’égard de la victime. À la question de savoir s’il avait consommé de l’alcool ou des stupéfiants au moment des faits, l’accusé répond par la négative. Il affirme avoir agi en pleine possession de ses facultés. Une circonstance relevée par le ministère public : après avoir commis son acte, l’accusé continuait de souffrir des mêmes maux qu’il imputait à sa cousine. Interrogé sur ce point par le procureur, il reconnaît que ses douleurs n’ont pas cessé. Aujourd’hui, S. D. dit regretter son geste. Le frère de la victime ne reconnaît aucun fait de sorcellerie À la barre, le frère de la victime apporte un éclairage sur la situation familiale de la défunte. Il indique que sa sœur vivait avec lui depuis le décès de son mari, il y a une vingtaine d’années. Il affirme n’avoir jamais entendu dire qu’elle pratiquait la sorcellerie et n’avoir jamais constaté de comportements allant dans ce sens. Pour le procureur du Faso près le tribunal de grande instance de Gaoua, les circonstances de la commission des faits permettent de retenir la préméditation. Estimant qu’aucune circonstance atténuante ne justifie une réduction de la responsabilité de l’accusé, il requiert contre S. D. la réclusion criminelle à perpétuité. À l’issue des débats, le dossier a été mis en délibéré. Source : Bafuji.infos.com L’article Gaoua : Convaincu que sa cousine l’avait ensorcelé, il la tue à coups de machette et risque la prison à vie est apparu en premier sur NetAfrique.net .

items.title: Power supply curtailed in parts of Kumasi as illegal logging damages GRIDCo line
items.description: Power supply to parts of the Western and Ashanti regions has been disrupted after illegal chainsaw operators felled a large tree onto a major 330kV transmission line operated by the Ghana Grid Company Limited (GRIDCo) . In a statement issued on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, GRIDCo said the 330kV transmission line running from Aboadze to Anwomaso tripped in the late afternoon, interrupting electricity supply . Following the trip, GRIDCo engineers patrolled the affected corridor and carried out investigations, which established that a large tree cut down by chainsaw operators had fallen onto the line and caused damage . Because of the unavailability of the critical transmission line, system operators have had to scale back power supplied to parts of Kumasi . GRIDCo stated that its engineers are working diligently to carry out repairs and restore the damaged line as quickly as possible . The company apologised to affected consumers for the inconvenience and assured the public that normal supply would resume once repair works are completed . items.title: Coup de tonnerre à la FBF : Rahim Ouédraogo quitte ses fonctions de 1er vice-président
items.description: Un vent de réorganisation souffle sur le sommet du football national au Burkina Faso. Dans une correspondance officielle adressée au président de la faîtière, le premier vice-président de la Fédération Burkinabè de Football (FBF), Rahim Assane Ouédraogo, a formellement présenté sa démission de ses fonctions pour des motifs de convenance personnelle. Membre du comité exécutif élu le 31 août 2024, le dirigeant met ainsi un terme à son mandat de manière anticipée, confiant la suite des affaires administratives à l'instance fédérale. L’instance dirigeante du ballon rond au Burkina Faso enregistre un départ majeur au sein de son exécutif. Dans une lettre officielle adressée à la Présidence de la Fédération Burkinabè de Football (FBF), le premier vice-président Rahim Assane Ouédraogo a notifié sa volonté de quitter immédiatement ses fonctions. Au cœur de cette démarche, le dirigeant a tenu à préciser qu'il s'agit d'une décision motivée exclusivement par des convenances personnelles, marquant ainsi en toute clarté les raisons de son retrait de l'instance dirigeante. Ce départ anticipé met fin à un parcours de plus de deux ans au sommet de la faîtière. Élu aux côtés de l'équipe fédérale lors de l'Assemblée générale du 31 août 2024, Rahim Ouédraogo aura cumulé exactement 807 jours de mandat (soit 2 ans, 2 mois et 16 jours) au service du football burkinabè. Tout au long de cette période, il a occupé le premier rang des vice-présidents, participant aux délibérations et aux orientations stratégiques du comité exécutif. La démission de Rahim Ouédraogo ouvre désormais une période d'ajustement administratif au sein du comité exécutif. En prenant acte de ce retrait motivé par des convenances personnelles, l'instance dirigeante de la FBF devra statuer sur la réorganisation de sa vice-présidence pour poursuivre la conduite des projets du football national. Dans les milieux sportifs du pays, ce départ retient l'attention des observateurs quant à la future configuration de l'équipe fédérale. items.title: Sénégal : Après avoir violé une prostituée, il accuse les « djinns » et risque 15 ans de prison
items.description: En détention provisoire depuis quatre ans à la suite d'une agression violente commise le 19 décembre 2022 à Joal, le pêcheur I. Faye a comparu devant la chambre criminelle du tribunal de Mbour. Accusé d'avoir violé une travailleuse du sexe sous la menace d'un gourdin, le prévenu a tenté de justifier son acte en invoquant la possession par des « djinns » avant de nier les faits à la barre. Face à la gravité des faits attestés par un certificat médical et au traumatisme de la victime, le procureur de la République a requis une peine exemplaire de 15 ans de réclusion criminelle. Le délibéré est attendu pour le 18 décembre prochain. La chambre criminelle du tribunal de Mbour s'est penchée sur une affaire d'agression sexuelle d'une extrême gravité. Les faits remontent à la nuit du 19 décembre 2022 dans la commune de Joal. Selon les éléments présentés à l'audience, I. Faye, un pêcheur originaire de Bargny, s'est rendu dans un établissement fréquenté par des travailleuses du sexe. Après s'être vu essuyer un refus de la part de deux femmes en raison d'une somme jugée insuffisante, le prévenu s'est introduit de force dans la chambre d'A. Diagne. Dissimulant un gourdin sous ses vêtements, il a menacé la jeune femme avant de la violer sans protection. Ce sont les cris de détresse de la victime qui ont alerté les vigiles d'un complexe voisin, lesquels sont intervenus pour défoncer la porte, maîtriser l'agresseur et le remettre aux gendarmes. Au cours de la procédure et lors de l'audience, les explications de l'accusé ont varié de manière déroutante. Lors de ses premières auditions durant l'enquête préliminaire, I. Faye avait reconnu les faits, affirmant avoir agi sous l’emprise de pulsions incontrôlables et de « djinns » après que la victime lui eut imposé le port d'un préservatif. À la barre du tribunal, l'accusé est toutefois revenu sur ses aveux, prétendant s'être simplement disputé avec la victime à la suite d'injures et n'avoir asséné qu'une gifle. Une version fermement contestée par le ministère public, qui a rappelé que les constatations médicales établies par l'hôpital de Mbour confirment sans ambiguïté les traces de violences et la réalité de l'agression sexuelle. Considérant la préméditation caractérisée par l'usage d'une arme et le mépris du consentement, le procureur a réclamé une sanction exemplaire. Dans son réquisitoire, le représentant du ministère public a insisté sur le fait que la profession ou la vulnérabilité sociale d'une femme ne saurait en aucun cas atténuer la responsabilité d'un agresseur ni justifier des actes de violence sexuelle. Rejetant les circonstances atténuantes et les alibis irrationnels, le parquet a requis 15 ans de réclusion criminelle à l'encontre d'I. Faye. Les juges ont mis l'affaire en délibéré et rendront leur verdict le 18 décembre prochain, dans un dossier qui remet au premier plan l'exigence d'une justice stricte face aux violences faites aux femmes au Sénégal. items.title: Culture/Burkina Faso : L’artiste DonSharp de Batoro rend hommage à la princesse Yennenga dans son 7ᵉ album
items.description: Le slameur et parolier burkinabè DonSharp de Batoro a présenté, le 24 novembre 2026 au Musée national de Ouagadougou, son septième album intitulé « Yennenga, la légende Poko ». Composé de 18 titres, cet opus met à l'honneur la princesse Yennenga et porte un message en faveur du leadership féminin, de l'entrepreneuriat et de la valorisation du patrimoine culturel africain. La musique au service de la mémoire historique et de la promotion de la femme. C'est autour de cette démarche que le slameur burkinabè DonSharp de Batoro a placé son nouvel album, « Yennenga, la légende Poko », présenté au public le mardi 24 novembre 2026 au Musée national de Ouagadougou. Avec ce septième opus, l'artiste consacre une œuvre entière à la princesse Yennenga, figure emblématique de l'histoire du royaume mossi. À travers 18 compositions, il entend faire connaître davantage le parcours de cette héroïne et promouvoir la femme comme actrice du développement et modèle de leadership. Yennenga, une figure historique au cœur du projet Artiste issu de la communauté gourounsi, DonSharp de Batoro a choisi de s'intéresser à une figure majeure du patrimoine mossi. Son projet retrace l'histoire de Yennenga, princesse réputée pour son courage, son indépendance et ses aptitudes guerrières. Après avoir consacré un précédent album à Soundiata Keïta, le slameur explique avoir voulu placer cette fois une figure féminine au centre de sa création. Pour lui, l'Afrique dispose de suffisamment de modèles historiques pour inspirer les générations actuelles, sans nécessairement chercher des références ailleurs. L'artiste résume sa démarche par cette déclaration : « Un peuple qui cesse de raconter son histoire risque de laisser d'autres la raconter à sa place. » À travers cette œuvre, il souhaite notamment encourager les femmes à s'inspirer de l'exemple de Yennenga dans les domaines du leadership, de l'entrepreneuriat et de l'autonomisation. Quatre années de travail pour 18 titres La réalisation de « Yennenga, la légende Poko » aura nécessité quatre années de travail, entre 2022 et 2026. Selon les explications de l'artiste, 47 maquettes ont été réalisées avec son arrangeur avant une sélection rigoureuse des morceaux. Au final, 17 titres ont été retenus, auxquels s'ajoute un morceau bonus consacré à la moto, portant le nombre total à 18. Présenté par son auteur comme le projet le plus abouti et le plus spirituel de sa carrière, l'album aborde plusieurs thématiques, notamment la spiritualité, les traditions gourounsi, les sonorités wagali, l'ego et les relations humaines. Le projet bénéficie également de collaborations avec des artistes tels que Nephtali, venu de Côte d'Ivoire, Frère Malkhom et Flowmanboy. L'album est disponible sur clé USB au prix de 10 000 FCFA. Le morceau principal, « Yennenga, la légende Poko », est également accompagné d'un vidéoclip officiel. De la création musicale à l'engagement social Pour DonSharp de Batoro, cet album ne se limite pas à une production musicale. Il constitue également un moyen de transmission de la mémoire collective et de valorisation du patrimoine africain. La démarche artistique s'accompagne d'une initiative sociale. L'artiste prévoit une série de formations consacrées au leadership féminin, à l'entrepreneuriat et à l'autonomisation des femmes. En mettant Yennenga au centre de cette initiative, le slameur entend faire de la mémoire historique un levier de sensibilisation et d'action en faveur des femmes. Avec « Yennenga, la légende Poko », DonSharp de Batoro associe ainsi création artistique, transmission culturelle et engagement social, dans une œuvre qui invite à redécouvrir les figures historiques africaines et à s'en inspirer pour construire l'avenir. items.title: Soldats ivoiriens en Haïti : Le gouvernement maintient le mystère
items.description: Interpellé ce mercredi 25 novembre 2026 à l’issue du Conseil des ministres sur la présence supposée de troupes ivoiriennes en Haïti, le porte-parole du gouvernement, Amadou Coulibaly, a maintenu une grande réserve, affirmant ne disposer d'aucune information officielle sur un tel déploiement. Alors que des sources concordantes évoquent l'envoi d'un contingent de militaires des Forces armées de Côte d'Ivoire (FACI) au sein de la mission internationale de sécurisation à Port-au-Prince, cette posture alimente les interrogations. Entre silence de l'état-major et débats sur l'opportunité d'une intervention extra-continentale, l'affaire suscite de vives réactions à Abidjan comme sur la scène internationale. Des soldats ivoiriens sont-ils engagés sur le sol haïtien ? La position officielle de l'exécutif ivoirien demeure pour l'instant entourée de mystère. Face aux journalistes réunis à l'issue du Conseil des ministres de ce mercredi 25 novembre 2026, le ministre de la Communication et porte-parole du gouvernement, Amadou Coulibaly, s'est montré particulièrement évasif lorsqu'il a été interrogé sur la présence de troupes des Forces armées de Côte d'Ivoire (FACI) dans les Caraïbes. « Déplacer des soldats ivoiriens sans que, de façon formelle, le gouvernement prenne la décision… Pour le moment, je n'en sais rien », a-t-il déclaré. En rappelant que tout mouvement de troupes à l'étranger obéit à des procédures institutionnelles et décisionnelles officielles, le ministre n'a ni confirmé ni formellement démenti la réalité de cette mission, laissant les observateurs dans l'attente d'une clarification formelle. Malgré cette réserve gouvernementale, les signaux d'un engagement militaire ivoirien se multiplient. Selon diverses sources d'information et des rapports spécialisés, un contingent d'environ 800 militaires ivoiriens aurait été préparé au camp d'Akouédo, bénéficiant d'une formation spécifique aux opérations de maintien de l'ordre, au combat urbain et au respect des droits humains. Ce déploiement s'inscrirait dans le cadre de la Mission multinationale d'appui à la sécurité (MMAS) en Haïti, soutenue par les Nations unies pour prêter main-forte à la police haïtienne face à l’emprise des gangs armés qui terrorisent Port-au-Prince. Après la phase initiale menée par le Kenya, l'intégration de troupes ivoiriennes constituerait un renfort de poids pour la force internationale. Cette perspective d'intervention hors du continent africain ne manque pas de soulever des débats passionnés. En Côte d'Ivoire, l'absence de communication détaillée de la part du ministère de la Défense et de l'état-major général des armées alimente les discussions au sein de la classe politique et de la société civile sur l'opportunité d'envoyer des troupes à plusieurs milliers de kilomètres. En Haïti également, le recours à des forces étrangères suscite des réticences auprès de plusieurs organisations citoyennes et politiques locales, qui remettent en cause l'efficacité des interventions extérieures. Alors que la situation sécuritaire en Haïti demeure critique, le gouvernement ivoirien se retrouve au centre des regards, appelé à clarifier la nature et le cadre juridique exacts de sa participation à cette opération internationale. L’article Soldats ivoiriens en Haïti : Le gouvernement maintient le mystère est apparu en premier sur NetAfrique.net .

items.title: Poundland collapses putting 11,000 jobs at risk
items.description: Poundland has collapsed into administration, putting 11,000 jobs at risk, after its owners failed to find a buyer to keep it in business. The retailer’s shops and distribution centres will remain open and continue trading during the administration process, with the business likely to be broken up and some stores sold to rival retailers. Poundland’s US owners held talks with several bidders over a last-minute rescue deal, but no agreement was reached. Poundland boss Barry Williams said in a note to staff that the board had “no alternative but to take this decision”, but was making it with “sincere sadness and intense regret”. He said the US owners Gordon Brothers had removed “all borrowing facilities and access to our bank accounts” on 27 October, and adequate funds had not been released since then to keep the business solvent. “Under these circumstances, it is impossible for the board of directors to see how Poundland can continue to operate as a going concern,” he added. ‘My income is gone’ Kelvin Blake, pictured at a protest in Walsall, has worked for Poundland for 25 years Kelvin Blake, 62, who has worked for the firm for 25 years, and whose partner has been there 29 years, said he was feeling “down, depressed”, and because of his age, feared he would not find a job elsewhere. “We didn’t want it, but it’s come so now we’ve just got to face it and see what the future holds. “My income’s gone,” he added. “Obviously, we’ll be working until we’re told to leave.” Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Poundland was “part of the fabric of high streets and communities up and down the country”. He said the news of it going into administration just weeks before Christmas would be “deeply concerning for workers and their families”. He added: “While it is worrying, going into administration does give other potential buyers the opportunity to engage, and we will work hard with all the relevant parties to ensure the best possible outcome.” Alix Partners, appointed administrator, said it would look at all options for the business, “including sales of the business and its assets, either in whole or part”. “We appreciate this is a deeply concerning time for all involved – customers, suppliers and, in particular, Poundland colleagues,” they said. Gordon Brothers has been criticised over how it handled a potential sale of Poundland, with accusations that the investment firm hoped to profit from selling off the chain’s 600 shops and stock piecemeal after running it into the ground. Gordon Brothers, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied such claims. On the funding question, Gordon Brothers said it had loaned the firm £85m over a year to help save it from insolvency. But insiders critical of the US firm have said it stands to make its loans back and more from the insolvency process. Previously, Gordon Brothers netted millions from liquidating the stock of fashion retailer LK Bennett, and in insolvency fees. Labour MP Liam Byrne told the BBC the House of Commons’ Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee will recall Gordon Brothers before Parliament – two weeks after Gordon Brothers representatives last appeared at the committee to answer questions about Poundland, and where MPs said they were “deeply concerned” about the business. Byrnesaid: “I am really worried that a ‘greed is good’ approach to business by its owners has forced [Poundland] into an administration.” He added the committee wants to know “how much money they’re ripping out and crucially, how do we make sure, as a country, that we don’t have this kind of scenario unfold again”. Gordon Brothers met Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds on Monday to update him on the progress. The firm said on Wednesday that despite Poundland management driving a turnaround over the past year, it was “still vulnerable” to inflation and any downturn in sales or profit margins, and had faced “several years of instability”. A spokesperson added the firm’s “thoughts are with Poundland colleagues”. It said it had stepped in to take over the retailer in 2025 when it was struggling, and when “no-one else was willing to finance the business”. One of the central stumbling blocks in negotiations to keep the business afloat was a shareholder loan Gordon Brothers inherited when it bought the business for less than £1 last year. Gordon Brothers owed £22.5m on that loan, while the previous owner, Pepco, owed £7.5m. Gordon Brothers rejected several offers to buy the business as a going concern, with deals to pay off the loan. Irish firm Martin Property Group offered to pay off £5m of the loan up front, and defer the rest of the payments to 2030. London-based Xyra Group offered £12.5m up front but ran out of time to close the deal. German investment firm Zachert Private Equity is also understood to have made a late offer. All of these were rejected. The crisis at Poundland really came to a head over the past few weeks after Gordon Brothers restricted access to funds for day-to-day operations. This meant the retailer’s stock wasn’t being replenished at the pace needed in the vital run-up to the festive period.

items.title: Shareholders back PBC’s GH¢300m debt restructuring plan
items.description: Shareholders of Produce Buying Company (PBC), Ghana’s largest licensed cocoa buying company, have approved a plan to raise GH¢300 million from the capital market to restructure the company’s finances and revive its cocoa purchasing operations. The approval was granted at an Extraordinary General Meeting (EGM) in Accra on Wednesday as the company seeks to address debts estimated at about GH¢673 million, including GH¢257 million owed to a consortium of banks, GH¢24 million owed to farmers for cocoa delivered since November 2025, and more than 20 months of salary arrears. Mr Seidu Yonye, Managing Director of PBC, told the Ghana News Agency after the meeting that the package comprised a GH¢100 million medium-term note from private investors and a GH¢200 million two-year commercial paper to be listed on the Ghana Stock Exchange. He said the GH¢100 million facility would be secured by the Golden Bean Hotel, a PBC subsidiary, as collateral. Mr Yonye said the financing would enable the company to reduce its bank debt, stabilise its finances and resume cocoa purchasing activities. He noted that pressure from outstanding bank obligations had led creditors to take legal action and threatened some of the company’s assets. “We want to go back into the market, purchase cocoa and make margins that will enable us to start resolving some of our debt portfolio,” he said. Mr Yonye said fund arrangers had substantially completed work on the GH¢100 million facility and were awaiting shareholder approval, which was required under corporate governance rules. “If we are able to pay GH¢100m, we’ll be reducing our debt portfolio by GH¢253 million, which is a very good gain made by PBC,” he said, referring to a debt restructuring agreement reached with the consortium of banks. Mr Yonye said the company had revalued its assets to strengthen its balance sheet and improve its attractiveness to investors. “These restructuring measures will return PBC to profitability, enable it to meet its obligations and eventually restore value to shareholders. We will do things differently to make sure that we sustain a vibrant and more profitable PBC for all shareholders and including the workers,” he said. Mr Samson Ashong, a shareholder, said the financing arrangements would help address the company’s long-standing financial challenges and support a return to core business operations. “For years, PBC has not been able to get any seed money to finance the purchasing of cocoa, where they get the margins for us to also benefit. Now that these financing arrangements are in place, we are excited because things will turn around. “The consortium of banks agreed to a haircut before the EGM, accepting less than what is owed because PBC’s finances were weak. They are now happy, expecting repayment, and will stop pursuing seizure of assets once paid,” he said. Mr Ashong urged management to prioritise repaying bank debts, clear workers’ salary arrears, and strengthen cocoa trading operations to improve profitability and restore shareholder value.

items.title: Malen penalty ends PSG’s perfect UCL run as Roma snatch 2-2 draw
items.description: Donyell Malen’s penalty gave Roma a 2-2 draw away to Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League on Wednesday, as the injury-hit reigning champions saw their perfect record in this season’s competition come to an end. Malen stroked in from the spot in the 78th minute on a bitterly cold and wet night at the Parc des Princes, giving Roma a welcome point after their collapse from two goals up to lose 3-2 at Manchester United last time out. Roma had earlier taken the lead through Mario Hermoso, only for Illia Zabarnyi to equalise before substitute Ousmane Dembele put PSG briefly in front with a penalty of his own. The result ends PSG’s perfect record in this season’s league phase, and halts a run of 12 consecutive wins in all competitions for Luis Enrique’s team. They fall two points behind Real Madrid, who are now clear at the top of the standings as the only side still with a 100 percent record after five matches. It is only a minor setback for PSG in their quest to finish in the top eight of the 36-team table, and therefore qualify directly for the last 16 without having to go through the play-off round like in the last two campaigns. But the Parisians could have done with the boost of a victory as they come to terms with the loss of the outstanding Desire Doue, who may not play again this season after rupturing the ACL in his right knee last weekend. Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, another of their outstanding attacking players, recently succumbed to the same injury, while Dembele has been struggling for fitness too and PSG’s prospects of winning a third straight Champions League title are undoubtedly diminished as a result. Dembele’s presence on the bench at kick-off meant that none of PSG’s five top scorers from last season were in their line-up here, with the others either injured or having departed in the case of Bradley Barcola and Goncalo Ramos. Meanwhile, Roma coach Gian Piero Gasperini raised eyebrows by leaving Malen out of his starting XI. The Dutchman is running at an average of more than a goal a game this season and netted four against Parma last weekend. – Dembele spot-kick – However, Roma have been in prolific form in general, netting 26 goals in their last seven matches before arriving in the French capital. They went ahead inside five minutes here as Matias Soule cut the ball back from the byline and Spanish defender Hermoso was on hand to convert. Roma had blown even more promising leads already this season, though, losing 4-3 at home to Real Madrid after leading 3-1 with eight minutes left, and then going down 3-2 at Old Trafford despite being 2-0 ahead at half-time. Ukrainian defender Zabarnyi levelled just after the half-hour mark as he found space at the near post to head in Senny Mayulu’s corner. Evan Ndicka headed just off-target for Roma late in the first half and Niccolo Pisilli forced a good stop from Matvei Safonov early in the second half. Joao Neves then headed agonisingly wide for PSG as he arrived unmarked in the area to meet a Nuno Mendes cross, before Dembele was introduced for the hosts in place of the ineffective Ferran Torres. Moments after that PSG won a penalty when Achraf Hakimi stormed into the Roma box only to be pulled down by Wesley. The French side had missed four penalties in the Champions League since the start of last season, but Dembele did score in the final against Arsenal in May. He kept a cool head to convert his fifth goal of the campaign, but PSG could not make it five straight Champions League wins this season. Malen entered the fray for Roma midway through the second half and looked on as Dembele was denied a brilliant solo goal by a Mile Svilar save. Roma then won a penalty following a VAR check after Vitinha blocked a Soule shot with a raised hand in the box. Up stepped Malen to score his 17th goal of a prolific campaign, boosting Roma’s hopes of reaching the knockout phase. items.title: Ghana’s legal framework for energy transition: Is the Renewable Energy Act, 2011 (ACT 832), fit for the country’s net-zero ambitions?
items.description: By: Ananpansah Bartholomew Abraham (AB) (DBE,LLB, BSC, MSC) 0241129910/0200704844 Abstract: Ghana’s commitment to achieving net-zero emissions by 2060 presents significant opportunities and challenges for the country’s energy sector. However, the principal legislation governing renewable energy development, the Renewable Energy Act, 2011 (Act 832), was enacted more than a decade before the country adopted its current long-term energy transition ambitions. This raises an important question as to whether the existing statutory framework is sufficiently equipped to facilitate the transition towards a low-carbon economy. This article critically examines the adequacy of Act 832, as amended by the Renewable Energy (Amendment) Act, 2020 (Act 1045), in advancing Ghana’s renewable energy and net-zero commitments. Through doctrinal legal analysis, it examines the relevant constitutional provisions, statutory framework, judicial decisions, international climate commitments and national energy policies. It argues that although Act 832 provides an important foundation for renewable energy development, its regulatory and promotional orientation falls short of establishing an enforceable decarbonisation framework. In particular, the absence of binding statutory renewable energy targets, the weakening of investment certainty following the amendment of the feed-in tariff regime, and the inadequate integration of climate obligations into renewable energy regulation undermine its effectiveness. The article consequently advocates statutory reform through enforceable renewable energy targets, improved electricity purchase guarantees, adequate financing mechanisms and stronger institutional coordination with Ghana’s climate governance framework. Keywords: Renewable Energy; Energy Transition; Net-Zero Emissions; Act 832; Climate Change; Ghana; Energy Law. Introduction The transition towards sustainable and low-carbon energy systems has become an important component of contemporary energy governance. Globally, governments are increasingly adopting legislative, regulatory and policy measures to reduce greenhouse gas emissions while ensuring energy security and sustainable economic development. Ghana is no exception. With considerable potential in solar, wind, biomass and other renewable energy resources, the country has an opportunity to diversify its energy mix and gradually reduce its dependence on fossil-fuel-based electricity generation. The constitutional foundation for environmental protection in Ghana is reflected in article 36(9) of the 1992 Constitution, which requires the State to take appropriate measures to protect and safeguard the national environment for posterity. This constitutional responsibility is reinforced by Ghana’s participation in international climate governance, particularly its ratification of the Paris Agreement in 2016 and the submission of its updated Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) in 2021. Under the updated NDC, Ghana committed to achieving an unconditional greenhouse gas emission reduction of 24.6 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (MtCO₂e) by 2030, with an additional 39.4 MtCO₂e reduction conditional on international support, bringing the overall target to 64 MtCO₂e.[1] Furthermore, Ghana’s Energy Transition and Investment Plan establishes a pathway towards achieving net-zero emissions by 2060. This ambition requires substantial changes in the production, distribution and consumption of energy, alongside the mobilisation of significant public and private investment. Notwithstanding these commitments, Ghana’s energy sector continues to face considerable dependence on thermal generation. The challenge, therefore, is not merely the availability of renewable energy resources or the existence of national policy commitments, but whether the country’s legal and regulatory institutions possess the necessary authority and mechanisms to translate those commitments into measurable outcomes. At the centre of this discussion is the Renewable Energy Act, 2011 (Act 832), as amended by the Renewable Energy (Amendment) Act, 2020 (Act 1045). Although the legislation provides a framework for promoting renewable energy development, its original design predates Ghana’s current net-zero ambition. This article examines whether the existing statutory framework is adequate to support Ghana’s energy transition. It contends that Act 832 remains largely a promotional and regulatory instrument rather than a comprehensive legislative framework for decarbonisation. It further argues that without targeted statutory reforms, Ghana’s net-zero commitments risk remaining policy aspirations rather than enforceable obligations. Methodology and Scope of the Study: This article adopts a doctrinal legal research methodology. It examines the relevant constitutional provisions, legislation, judicial decisions, international instruments and national energy policy documents to assess the legal and institutional foundations of Ghana’s renewable energy transition. Particular attention is given to Act 832 and its 2020 amendment, the constitutional provisions governing environmental protection and international business transactions, and the implications of relevant Supreme Court decisions for renewable energy investment. The analysis also draws on Ghana’s updated NDC, the Energy Transition and Investment Plan, the Renewable Energy Master Plan and relevant academic commentary. The objective is to determine whether the existing legal framework creates sufficiently clear, enforceable and financially sustainable obligations to facilitate the country’s transition towards net-zero emissions. Ghana’s Legal and Institutional Framework for Renewable Energy Development: 3.1 The Renewable Energy Act, 2011 (Act 832) Act 832 constitutes the principal legislative framework for the development, management and utilisation of renewable energy resources in Ghana. Section 1 identifies its central objective as facilitating the development and utilisation of renewable energy sources for the production of heat and power in an efficient and environmentally sustainable manner. The Act also seeks to create an enabling environment for investment, diversify energy supply, improve electricity access, promote indigenous technological capacity and encourage public education on renewable energy. Institutionally, the legislation provides for regulatory oversight by the Energy Commission, while the Public Utilities Regulatory Commission (PURC) performs important functions relating to electricity pricing and tariffs. The significance of Act 832 cannot be understated. It provides the legal foundation upon which renewable energy generation, licensing, procurement and grid integration are regulated. Nevertheless, its principal orientation is the promotion and orderly regulation of renewable energy development rather than the imposition of legally enforceable emissions reduction obligations. This distinction becomes particularly important when the legislation is assessed against Ghana’s 2060 net-zero ambition. 3.2 The Renewable Energy (Amendment) Act, 2020 (Act 1045) The 2020 amendment substantially restructured the renewable energy procurement framework. Under the amended section 25, a competitive procurement scheme was introduced, comprising tendering and auction arrangements. The amendment requires renewable electricity procurement by public utilities to follow an open, competitive and transparent process. It also empowers the Energy Commission, in consultation with the PURC, to determine procurement targets as part of annual energy supply and demand plans. Section 26 was similarly revised. It provides for the procurement of electricity from consumer generators under a net-metering arrangement and requires certain fossil-fuel-based electricity suppliers and other companies contributing to greenhouse gas emissions to invest in non-utility-scale renewable energy projects to offset emissions and mitigate climate change. Additionally, section 30A establishes a net-metering scheme intended to encourage self-generation of renewable electricity for electricity cost reduction or climate change mitigation, rather than income generation. One of the most significant consequences of the amendment, however, was the repeal of sections 27 to 29, together with the removal of the original feed-in tariff framework. Although competitive procurement can promote efficiency and reduce procurement costs, the removal of guaranteed tariff arrangements raises concerns about investment certainty. This is particularly relevant in renewable energy projects, which often require substantial initial capital investment and long-term revenue predictability. Consequently, the amendment presents a regulatory tension between achieving competitive electricity procurement and maintaining sufficient financial incentives to attract renewable energy investors. Critical Assessment of Act 832 Against Ghana’s Net-Zero Commitments: The adequacy of Act 832 must be assessed not merely by reference to its original objectives but also by considering the demands of Ghana’s present energy transition commitments. Three principal weaknesses emerge from this assessment. 4.1 Absence of Binding Statutory Renewable Energy Targets A fundamental weakness of Act 832 is the absence of a clear, legally binding national renewable electricity target directly linked to Ghana’s net-zero commitments. Although section 25(3) of the amended Act empowers the Energy Commission, in consultation with the PURC, to determine procurement targets as part of annual energy supply and demand plans, the legislation does not establish a comprehensive statutory renewable electricity trajectory with specific long-term milestones. The Renewable Energy Master Plan, for instance, identifies a renewable energy penetration target of 10 per cent and an installed capacity ambition of approximately 1,363.63 MW by 2030. However, these targets are contained in policy instruments rather than being expressly entrenched as binding obligations under Act 832. The distinction between statutory obligations and policy aspirations is important. While policy documents provide strategic direction, their implementation may depend substantially on administrative discretion, political priorities and available resources. Consequently, the absence of a clearly enforceable statutory target weakens accountability and makes it difficult to measure the extent to which relevant public institutions are legally required to deliver the country’s renewable energy ambitions. A legislative framework designed to support a net-zero transition should go beyond encouraging renewable energy investment. It should establish measurable obligations against which institutional performance can be assessed. 4.2 Weakening of Investment Certainty Following the Removal of the Feed-in Tariff Framework A second concern relates to the removal of the original feed-in tariff framework through Act 1045. The feed-in tariff arrangement under the original Act was intended to guarantee the purchase of electricity generated from renewable energy sources through a structured purchase obligation and regulated tariff mechanism. The repeal of the relevant provisions in 2020 fundamentally changed the investment environment. Although the competitive procurement framework introduced by the amendment may encourage cost efficiency, it does not necessarily provide the same degree of revenue certainty associated with a guaranteed tariff arrangement. Renewable energy projects are generally capital-intensive and require predictable revenue streams to attract long-term financing. Where investors are uncertain about procurement arrangements, pricing mechanisms and the availability of enforceable purchase commitments, the cost of capital may increase and project development may become less attractive. Furthermore, although section 26(3) imposes an investment obligation on certain fossil-fuel-related companies to support non-utility-scale renewable energy projects, the effectiveness of this provision depends on the determination and implementation of the relevant investment requirements. The absence of sufficiently clear implementation timelines and effective enforcement mechanisms raises questions about the practical impact of the obligation. Similarly, the net-metering framework under section 30A is primarily intended to support electricity cost reduction and climate mitigation rather than commercial electricity generation. While this is a useful mechanism for encouraging decentralised renewable energy adoption, it cannot independently provide the scale of investment required for Ghana’s broader energy transition. The financing challenge is further compounded by concerns surrounding the operational effectiveness and capitalisation of the Renewable Energy Fund. A fund without predictable and adequate financial resources cannot effectively reduce investment barriers or support the development of commercially viable renewable energy projects. 4.3 Constitutional and Contractual Uncertainty in Renewable Energy Investment A further issue concerns the constitutional requirements governing international business transactions involving the Government of Ghana. Article 181(5) of the 1992 Constitution provides that the provisions of article 181 relating to loans shall, with the necessary modifications, apply to international business or economic transactions to which the Government is a party. The Supreme Court’s decision in Attorney-General v Faroe Atlantic Co Ltd demonstrates the importance of parliamentary approval in the enforcement of qualifying international business transactions. The decision established that transactions falling within article 181(5) require the constitutionally prescribed parliamentary approval. The Supreme Court subsequently considered the application of this constitutional requirement in Republic v High Court (Commercial Division), Accra; Ex parte Attorney-General (Balkan Energy Ghana Ltd and Others Interested Parties). The proceedings concerned a power purchase agreement between the Government of Ghana and Balkan Energy Ghana Limited and the constitutional implications of the absence of parliamentary approval. These decisions have important implications for renewable energy investment, particularly where projects involve foreign investors, government-backed power purchase agreements or other international commercial arrangements. Although parliamentary approval serves an important constitutional accountability function, uncertainty regarding the application and timing of the approval process may create additional risks for investors and financiers. Act 832 does not adequately address this constitutional dimension of renewable energy project development. A comprehensive energy transition framework should therefore incorporate clear procedures and institutional safeguards to ensure that relevant power purchase agreements and international investment arrangements satisfy constitutional requirements from the outset. The Relationship Between Ghana’s Renewable Energy Legislation and Climate Governance: The assessment of Act 832 would be incomplete without considering the broader climate governance framework. Ghana’s obligations under the Paris Agreement and its updated NDC establish an important international and national policy foundation for emissions reduction. However, international climate commitments must be supported by domestic legislative and institutional arrangements capable of facilitating implementation. The Environmental Protection Act, 2025 (Act 1124), represents an important development in this regard. Among other things, the legislation establishes the Ghana Carbon Registry under section 150 and provides for the establishment of a Carbon Market Committee under section 151. These provisions create an institutional foundation for the registration, tracking and coordination of carbon market activities and internationally transferred mitigation outcomes. The existence of this framework presents an opportunity to strengthen the relationship between renewable energy regulation and climate governance. For instance, renewable energy projects may contribute to national emissions reduction objectives while also participating in appropriately regulated carbon market arrangements. However, such opportunities require coordination between the institutions responsible for energy regulation, environmental protection and carbon market administration. The absence of an express and comprehensive statutory relationship between Act 832 and Ghana’s wider climate governance framework creates the possibility of regulatory fragmentation. It is therefore necessary to ensure that renewable energy legislation is aligned with the Environmental Protection Act, 2025, and Ghana’s evolving climate policy architecture. Independent Assessment and Proposed Legal Reforms: In my assessment, the central difficulty with Act 832 is not necessarily the absence of political commitment to renewable energy development, but rather the limitations of its legislative design. The Act was enacted primarily to promote and regulate renewable energy development. However, the demands of a net-zero transition require a more comprehensive framework that establishes clear legal responsibilities, measurable targets, predictable investment conditions and effective accountability mechanisms. Four principal reforms are therefore recommended. 6.1 Introduction of Binding Renewable Energy Targets. Parliament should consider amending Act 832 to introduce clearly defined and legally binding renewable electricity targets, supported by measurable interim milestones towards 2030, 2040, 2050 and 2060. Such targets should be aligned with Ghana’s NDC and long-term net-zero commitments. The Minister responsible for Energy should also be required to submit annual reports to Parliament detailing progress, implementation challenges and corrective measures. This would strengthen institutional accountability and transform renewable energy targets from largely policy-driven aspirations into statutory obligations. 6.2 Restoration of a Bankable Renewable Energy Purchase Mechanism Ghana should consider introducing a more reliable renewable energy purchase obligation capable of providing investors with reasonable revenue certainty. This need not necessarily involve a wholesale return to the previous feed-in tariff regime. Rather, Parliament could adopt a balanced mechanism combining competitive procurement with regulated minimum purchase guarantees or other enforceable long-term offtake arrangements. The obligation should extend beyond limited consumer-generator arrangements and provide a sufficiently broad demand-side framework for commercially viable renewable energy projects. Such an approach would preserve the benefits of competitive procurement while addressing the investment uncertainty associated with the removal of the original feed-in tariff framework. 6.3 Adequate Capitalisation of the Renewable Energy Fund The Renewable Energy Fund must be supported by a predictable and sustainable financing mechanism. Government should consider allocating a defined proportion of appropriate existing energy-related levies or other designated public revenue sources to the Fund. Clear eligibility criteria, transparent disbursement procedures and regular financial reporting should also be established. The Fund should prioritise projects that address financing barriers, support indigenous renewable energy enterprises, promote decentralised electricity generation and improve access to clean energy in underserved communities. A properly capitalised Renewable Energy Fund would help reduce the financial risks associated with renewable energy development and strengthen private-sector participation. 6.4 Integration of Renewable Energy Regulation with Climate Legislation Act 832 should be expressly aligned with the Environmental Protection Act, 2025 (Act 1124), particularly its provisions establishing the Ghana Carbon Registry and Carbon Market Committee. This alignment should provide a coordinated framework for renewable energy project registration, emissions accounting, carbon market participation and the verification of climate benefits. It should also clarify the respective responsibilities of the Energy Commission, PURC, Environmental Protection Authority and other relevant institutions. In addition, the constitutional requirements governing international business transactions should be addressed through clearer administrative procedures to minimise uncertainty in the negotiation and approval of renewable energy investment agreements. Finally, where statutory environmental and climate-related obligations are ignored or inadequately implemented, affected persons may explore appropriate constitutional and judicial remedies. In this regard, the Supreme Court’s decision in Ghana Lotto Operators Association v National Lottery Authority is relevant for its recognition of a presumption of justiciability in relation to certain Directive Principles of State Policy. Nevertheless, the application of that principle to specific energy transition obligations would require careful judicial consideration. Conclusion: Ghana has made significant commitments towards renewable energy development and the achievement of a low-carbon economy. The 2060 net-zero ambition, together with the country’s international climate commitments, demonstrates the importance of transitioning towards a more sustainable energy system. However, the existence of ambitious policy commitments does not automatically translate into effective legal implementation. The Renewable Energy Act, 2011 (Act 832), remains an important foundation for renewable energy regulation in Ghana. Nevertheless, its promotional and regulatory orientation, coupled with the limitations introduced by the 2020 amendment, raises legitimate concerns about its adequacy in supporting the country’s current net-zero ambitions. The absence of comprehensive binding statutory targets, insufficient investment certainty, financing limitations and inadequate integration with the broader climate governance framework all point to the need for legislative reform. Ultimately, Ghana’s energy transition requires more than policy declarations and institutional encouragement. It requires a coherent legal framework that establishes enforceable obligations, mobilises sustainable financing, protects legitimate investor expectations and strengthens institutional accountability. The future effectiveness of Ghana’s net-zero commitments will therefore depend, to a considerable extent, on whether the country is prepared to move beyond a predominantly promotional renewable energy regime towards a legally enforceable and financially sustainable framework for decarbonisation. items.title: Women lawyers have a big role in law reforms – Ayine
items.description: Dr Dominic Akuritinga Ayine, Attorney General and Minister of Justice, expressed confidence that including women lawyers in law reform processes in Ghana and across Africa would accelerate legal development and strengthen access to justice. He said that although law reform is a demanding undertaking, a shared commitment and unity of purpose could catalyse meaningful progress. Dr Ayine was speaking at the African Women Lawyers Association (AWLA) International Conference in Accra on the theme: “Better Together, AWLA Beaming Her Light on: Create, Empower, Prosper, Together in Africa.” The Attorney General said the Intestate Succession Bill, currently before Parliament, was designed to address longstanding gaps in Ghana’s inheritance laws by establishing a uniform intestate succession regime applicable throughout the country. He noted that four decades after enacting PNDC Law 111, sufficient experience had been gained to identify weaknesses in the legislation and develop measures to address them. “Last year PNDC Law 111 turned 40, and 40 years is long enough to see a law’s gaps clearly. Its fractional formula has proved difficult to apply. Its treatment of the matrimonial home does not fit families with more than one house or more than one spouse,” he stated. Dr Ayine explained that the law did not adequately address issues relating to polygamous marriages, dependent parents and children still in school who depended on deceased breadwinners. “It does not yet provide one coherent rule for every Ghanaian regardless of the inheritance system of their family or the type of marriage they contracted,” he added. According to him, the Intestate Succession Bill replaces the existing fractional distribution formula with a percentage-sharing system and introduces provisions that better respond to the needs of immediate family members. “The Bill has passed its second reading. It has been before successive Parliaments, in one form or another, since 2009, when my predecessor, Betty Mould-Iddrissu, laid it before Parliament, and it is time to finish the work,” he indicated. Dr Ayine said women lawyers across Ghana and Africa had played a pivotal role in advancing reforms relating to intestate succession, women’s property rights and the protection of children’s rights. He commended AWLA for its contributions over the past three decades to advancing justice, legal reform, and women’s empowerment. Speaking at the conference, Madam Gloria Ofori-Boadu, President of the International Federation of Women Lawyers (FIDA)-Ghana, called on women in the judiciary and civil society organisations to champion increased marriage registration across Ghana and Africa. “We need to champion accessible, reasonable and affordable registration of marriages,” she urged. Madam Ofori-Boadu observed that many people still held the misconception that marriage registration was optional and stressed the need to promote compliance with registration requirements. She noted that Africa’s prosperity could not be achieved in isolation, adding that marriage registration would not only economically empower women but also strengthen family structures and enhance legal protection for spouses. The FIDA-Ghana President further stated that sustainable development and empowerment could not be realised while women, girls and families continued to face discrimination, inequality and violence in various spheres of socio-economic life.

items.title: UCL: Pochettino still winless as Man United draw 2-2 with Sporting
items.description: Mauricio Pochettino must wait for his first win as Manchester United coach after a wild 2-2 Champions League draw at Sporting Lisbon on Wednesday, with the hosts equalising thanks to a goalkeeping error from Senne Lammens. The Belgian stopper’s poor handling allowed Luis Suarez to complete a brace for the hosts, cancelling out United playmaker Bruno Fernandes’s double against his former side. United gave away two penalties in the first half, the second converted by Suarez, before Fernandes equalised from the spot early in the second half. Fernandes sent United ahead with a lucky bounce taking his effort over the Sporting goalkeeper, before Suarez’s acrobatic effort levelled the game. United midfielder Youri Tielemans was sent off in stoppage time for a second yellow card to end a compelling and often erratic match. A crushing 4-0 defeat by rivals Liverpool in the Premier League at the weekend, leaving United 19th, was a disastrous first game at the helm for Pochettino after replacing Michael Carrick. Pochettino brought Harry Maguire into the three-man defence as he shuffled his pack, as well as starting Joshua Zirkzee in place of the suspended Matheus Cunha. Neither side took many risks in the opening stages, with few chances of note until the game burst into life midway through the first half as United lost control. Lisandro Martinez brought down Geny Catamo in the area and Sporting were awarded a penalty. The hosts blew their chance from the spot, with Suarez’s scuffed effort easily saved by Lammens, but the Red Devils gave away another spot kick just a couple of minutes later. Goalkeeper Lammens came flying off his line and clattered Maxi Araujo, and this time Colombian striker Suarez made no mistake from the spot. – United unhappy with disallowed goals – United thought they had equalised when Amad Diallo hit the crossbar and then nodded home the rebound, but the goal was disallowed to their dismay. Youri Tielemans was ruled to have fouled Goncalo Inacio, although he seemed to win the ball, upsetting United further after Leny Yoro’s controversial red card against Liverpool on Sunday that was later rescinded. Fernandes pulled United level early in the second half from the spot after Eduardo Quaresma brought down Martinez. The former Sporting playmaker calmly stroked his penalty beyond the dive of Kaique Pereira into the bottom left corner. Fernandes said on the eve of the game he had stopped contract talks because he wanted to focus on helping United improve their form after a dire start to the season. The midfielder soon had his second goal, with the help of a bizarre bounce off a divot on the pitch. Fernandes’s low effort from distance seemed bound for Pereira’s hands, but suddenly bounced up off a patch of uneven turf and fortuitously over the goalkeeper’s head. The Portugal international bent a free-kick narrowly off target as he looked to complete his hat-trick. Lammens saved well from Sergi Altimira to protect United’s lead as Sporting battled to find an equaliser. It eventually came from a howler from Lammens, who failed to claim a cross dropping out of the sky, spilling the ball in front of Suarez, who produced a hooked acrobatic effort to score. Moments later United had the ball in the net at the other end after another goalkeeping error by Pereira, who mishandled Fernandes’s corner, pushing the ball into his own net. However what would have been the winner was disallowed for an elbow by Patrick Dorgu on the goalkeeper, a decision the visitors were also unhappy about. Dangote Refinery to list on Nigerian Exchange December 1
items.description: The Dangote Petroleum Refinery says it will begin trading on the Nigerian Exchange (NGX) Group on December 1, marking its entry into the Nigerian stock market following its initial public offering (IPO). Devakumar Edwin, vice-president of oil and gas at Dangote Group, announced the development on Wednesday, according to a Reuters report. The listing comes after the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) approved the refinery’s share allocation plan following its heavily oversubscribed IPO, which closed last month. The regulatory approval cleared the way for the company to distribute shares to investors and proceed with preparations for its stock market debut. The refinery had earlier sought to increase the size of its IPO by up to 30 per cent to approximately $2.1 billion following strong investor demand. On September 11, Aliko Dangote, president of Dangote Industries Limited (DIL), said the refinery planned to pursue a listing on a United States stock exchange after expanding its production capacity to 1.4 million barrels per day within the next two and a half years. However, on November 8, Dangote disclosed that the refinery’s IPO fell short of its target of attracting 10 million investors. Despite missing the target, Africa’s richest person said the offer attracted “millions of investors”. He described the level of participation as significant when compared with some of the largest public offerings in Africa and globally. items.title: Gunshots heighten tension at Nyanyano over chieftaincy dispute
items.description: Residents of Gomoa Nyanyano in the Gomoa East District of the Central Region have been thrown into fear following reports of sporadic gunfire amid escalating tensions over a planned homecoming celebration by traditional authorities. The latest unrest is linked to a protracted chieftaincy dispute that has unsettled the community since the death of its former chief, Nana Obeng Wiabor V. The planned ceremony has reportedly met resistance from some residents, who fear that holding the event could deepen divisions among rival factions and trigger further violence. Tensions escalated after a group of residents allegedly gathered at the palace of the deceased chief to protest the planned celebration. An official vehicle belonging to the traditional authorities was subsequently set ablaze. The incident reportedly led to the arrest of some suspects, sparking anger among sections of the community. The situation is said to have deteriorated further, with agitated residents allegedly attempting to attack the Nyanyano Police Station as gunshots rang out in parts of the town. The latest developments have raised concerns about a possible escalation of the conflict, with residents worried about their safety and the security of property. The violence comes barely a day after reports emerged that an official vehicle belonging to the traditional authorities had been torched at the Gomoa Nyanyano Chief’s Palace in the early hours of Tuesday, November 24. An eyewitness, Kweku Botwey, narrated that the suspected attackers had earlier threatened to set the palace ablaze over the planned homecoming celebration. He alleged that masked individuals poured petrol on the vehicle before setting it on fire and fleeing. Nyanyano has a history of violent confrontations over the chieftaincy question. In December 2025, clashes between rival factions left two people injured, prompting the deployment of more than 50 police officers and other security personnel to restore order. In February 2026, another attack involving more than 100 people reportedly resulted in vandalism at the community palace. Ten suspects were arrested following that incident. The dispute also disrupted an Easter convention organised by the Church of Pentecost in April 2026, when suspected land guards reportedly invaded the venue and dismantled canopies. The police subsequently suspended public activities in the area as a precautionary measure.

items.title: Mahama pays last respect to late Agogomanhene Nana Kwame Akuoku Sarpong
items.description: President John Mahama on Wednesday joined the family, chiefs, and people of Asante Akyem Agogo, as well as Asanteman, to bid farewell to the late Agogomanhene, Nana Kwame Akuoku Sarpong II, at the Ofori ne Krobon Palace (also known as the Kyei ne Krobon Palace) in Agogo, Ashanti Region. The President was received at the palace by the Paramount Queen Mother of Asante Akyem Agogo (Agogohenemaa), Nana Juaben Afrakoma Serwaa Kusi Oboadum. President Mahama donated GH¢600,000.00 towards the funeral of the late Agogomanhene. Speaking through Dr Frank Amoakohene, Ashanti Regional Minister, the President eulogised Nana Akuoku Sarpong for his immense contributions to Ghana’s development. He said the late Agogomanhene served the nation in various capacities, including as Minister of Health, Minister for the Interior and a Member of the Council of State. The President reiterated that Ghana’s history could not be written without acknowledging Nana Akuoku Sarpong’s significant contributions to national development. Nana Akuoku Sarpong passed away on March 26, 2026, at 87, after a distinguished 51-year reign. His three-day Dɔte Yie (final funeral and burial rites), which began on November 24, will end on November 26, 2026, in Agogo. The funeral has attracted dignitaries from across the country, including traditional rulers, political leaders, family members and well-wishers who gathered to honour the memory of the revered chief and statesman.

items.title: Foot: la Mauritanie se sépare d’Aritz López Garai et de son staff, les candidatures sont ouvertes
items.description: Réuni en session extraordinaire, le Conseil de la Fédération mauritanienne de football a annoncé la fin des contrats du sélectionneur et de son encadrement technique. La date limite des candidatures pour sa succession est fixée au 10 décembre. NOUAKCHOTT – La Fédération mauritanienne de football (FFRIM) et son sélectionneur Aritz López Garai ont mis fin à leur collaboration. Le Conseil de la FFRIM l'a annoncé dans un communiqué daté du mercredi 25 novembre 2026, à l'issue d'une session extraordinaire tenue le soir même par visioconférence. La réunion avait pour objet d'examiner la situation de l'équipe nationale A. À son terme, le Conseil indique être « parvenu à un accord à l'amiable » avec le technicien et les membres de son staff pour résilier leurs contrats respectifs. Le communiqué ne précise ni les motifs de cette décision ni les conditions financières de la séparation. Dans le même texte, la fédération remercie Aritz López Garai et son encadrement pour leur engagement et le travail accompli au service des Mourabitounes. Elle leur souhaite « pleine réussite » pour la suite de leur parcours professionnel. Un appel à candidatures lancé immédiatement Le Conseil annonce l'ouverture des candidatures au poste de sélectionneur de l'équipe nationale A, à compter de la publication du communiqué. Les dossiers doivent être envoyés au plus tard le 10 décembre 2026, soit environ quinze jours, à l'adresse électronique candidatures@ffrim.org. La FFRIM ne dit rien, à ce stade, du calendrier de la sélection ni de l'identité de la personne qui assurera l'intérim d'ici la nomination du nouveau sélectionneur. Elle n'indique pas non plus les critères attendus des candidats.
