items.title: Produits forestiers non-ligneux, une niche insoupçonnée (Par Malick CISS)
items.description: Les ressources végétales sauvages de nos forêts et brousses constituent une niche stratégique pour l’industrialisation rurale et les exportations, à côté de leur fonction dans la sécurité alimentaire. La consommation de ces produits forestiers non-ligneux est tellement entrée dans nos habitudes alimentaires et médicinales, qu’on en arrive à perdre de vue leur valeur économique. Nous nous apercevons de l’importance de ces ressources cantonnées à la cueillette que quand nous en avons besoin. Kinkéliba, bissap, pain de singe ou « bouy », « soump » sont pourtant des produits très prisés par l’industrie cosmétique et agroalimentaire. La plupart de ces produits vendus à l’état brut gagnent de plus en plus de la place dans l’industrie cosmétique et agroalimentaire, qui a découvert sur le tard leurs propriétés. Le marché du beurre de karité, par exemple, pèse près de 3,4 milliards de dollars en 2026 au niveau mondial, avec des projections dépassant les cinq milliards à l’horizon 2034, selon Business Research Insights, spécialisé dans les études de marché. Plus près de nous, on peut citer la noix de cajou, secteur en pleine croissance et à fort potentiel économique, qui rentre dans la production d’huile ou de lait hydratant, la fabrication de savon, de lubrifiant (résine de la coque), dont une bonne partie de la production (plus de 90 %) est exportée à l’état brut. Que dire du bissap, au marché mondial en constante évolution pour une valorisation industrielle pour ses vertus nutritives (antioxydant, diurétique, digestion, etc.). La demande mondiale de bissap, en forte expansion, connaît une croissance annuelle estimée entre 6 et 10,7 % et une hausse globale de 25 % depuis 2021, notamment en Europe et aux États-Unis, selon la chercheuse en agroéconomie, Atoumasamba Sissoko (in L’hibiscus africain -Hibiscus sabdariffa- : propriétés santé, dynamiques de marché et défis pour les producteurs africains). La fondatrice de la marque Trésors d’Afrique explique cet engouement par une sensibilisation aux bienfaits des superaliments, les alternatives aux sodas, une intégration croissante dans l’industrie cosmétique (propriétés anti-âge et hydratantes). Un autre produit très utilisé dans l’industrie cosmétique, parapharmaceutique et agroalimentaire, c’est le très négligé « soump » que nous utilisons juste pour ses vertus laxatives. Avec son huile très riche, il est recherché dans les pays occidentaux pour ses soins anti-âge, les crèmes hydratantes et les produits capillaires. On allait oublier le moringa (nébéday), très en vogue pour ses nombreuses vertus (nutrition, complément alimentaire, huile de la graine très recherchée en cosmétique), au marché mondial évalué à 11 milliards de dollars cette année et à 25,2 milliards à l’horizon 2034. On ne saurait clore la liste (loin d’être exhaustive) sans parler du pain de singe ou « bouy », qui constitue un segment estimé à plus de 100 millions de dollars en 2026, avec une projection de 173 millions à l’horizon 2031, selon la société d’étude Mordor Intelligence. Business Insight estime la taille du marché mondial des produits dérivés du baobab (poudre, pulpe, huile, etc., utilisés comme aliments et boissons, la cosmétique) à 5,74 milliards de dollars en 2025 et à 10,62 milliards d’ici à 2034. En 2025, le gros bénéficiaire de ce marché, c’est… l’Amérique du Nord qui a empoché 30 % des revenus l’année dernière. La valeur ajoutée de ces produits est souvent captée par les pays développés, l’Afrique se contentant des maigres recettes générées par les exportations de matières brutes. Il urge aujourd’hui d’investir dans le conditionnement et la transformation de ces produits pour capter davantage de valeur ajoutée, créer des emplois en assurant l’approvisionnement constant du marché mondial. Des efforts sont en train d’être faits, certes (notamment pour la noix de cajou, le bissap, le moringa), mais nous devons aller à la conquête de marchés nouveaux. Mais les défis sont nombreux, le premier étant de sortir de l’informel pour mieux structurer l’offre et surtout créer une industrie de transformation. Une structuration des filières permet d’approvisionner le marché mondial en permanence, en s’affranchissant de la collecte sauvage ou saisonnière. Répondre aux exigences sanitaires, douanières et de traçabilité constituent autant d’obstacles à lever. Et aussi affiner la recherche scientifique pour une meilleure connaissance de ces produits que nous négligeons, mais qui sont des niches peu explorées. malick.ciss@lesoleil.sn

items.title: CAMES 2026 : la Guinée célèbre ses 34 nouveaux maîtres de conférences agrégés
items.description: L'Université Gamal Abdel Nasser de Conakry (UGANC) a accueilli une cérémonie officielle consacrant les lauréats guinéens du 23e concours d'agrégation du Conseil africain et malgache pour l'enseignement supérieur (CAMES) en médecine humaine, pharmacie, odontostomatologie, médecine vétérinaire et productions animales, organisé du 10 au 18 novembre 2026 à Bangui, en République centrafricaine. Sur 40 candidats présentés, 34 ont été déclarés admis au grade de maître de conférences agrégé, soit un taux de réussite de 85 % répartis dans 23 spécialités. Ouvrant la série d'interventions, le recteur de l'UGANC, le Pr Alpha Kabinet Keita, a salué une victoire partagée par l'université et la nation, fruit d'années de travail clinique, de recherche et d'abnégation. Il a rappelé que l'agrégation impose des devoirs immédiats d'encadrement, de publication sous affiliation institutionnelle et de service aux patients. S'appuyant sur la publication du classement universitaire 2027, le Pr Alpha Kabinet Keita a noté que l'UGANC maintient la tête des universités guinéennes pour la troisième année consécutive, avec un score passé de 71/100 en 2025 et 2026 à 78,0/100 en 2027, tout en appelant à renforcer la visibilité de la recherche et les partenariats internationaux dans le cadre du futur plan stratégique 2027-2032. Le doyen de la Faculté de médecine, le Pr Mohamed Cissé, a, pour sa part, souligné la complexité de l'épreuve du CAMES, où les candidats doivent faire valoir la valeur de leurs travaux, la rigueur scientifique et leurs aptitudes pédagogiques devant des jurys souverains, tout en mettant en avant le suivi des candidats et le rôle des universitaires guinéens impliqués dans le processus. Prenant la parole au nom des 34 lauréats, la porte-parole des agrégés, Dr Aissatou Barry, a exprimé sa gratitude envers Dieu, les encadreurs, les familles et le gouvernement pour l'accompagnement de la délégation guinéenne. Elle a également adressé un message fraternel aux candidats non admis, les assurant de la disponibilité des nouveaux agrégés pour les prochaines sessions, avant de remettre symboliquement le drapeau. Clôturant la cérémonie, la ministre de l'Enseignement supérieur et de la Recherche scientifique, Djami Diallo, après avoir transmis les salutations du président de la République, Mamadi Doumbouya, et du Premier ministre, a salué la réussite des 34 lauréats, exprimé sa reconnaissance aux six candidats non retenus, remercié le CAMES et les autorités centrafricaines, et rappelé la vocation intégrée de l'institution créée en 1968. La ministre a fixé quatre priorités aux nouveaux maîtres de conférences agrégés, à savoir : l'exemplarité pédagogique et clinique dans les amphithéâtres comme au chevet des malades, une recherche active et productive au service du rayonnement scientifique national, la formation des formateurs et l'émergence d'écoles scientifiques capables d'asseoir la présence guinéenne dans les jurys du CAMES, l'éthique et la déontologie comme socle indispensable de la compétence. Elle a enfin assuré que le gouvernement, en lien avec les ministères de la Santé et de la Fonction publique, veillera à la prise en compte de ce nouveau grade dans les carrières et l'organisation des établissements, tout en renforçant la préparation des futures cohortes.

items.title: How Did Any Child Survive the 1970s?
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In this week’s episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum is joined by the author and journalist Meghan Cox Gurdon to discuss her new memoir, Free Range Girl , about growing up in the 1970s. They explore how parenting has changed, the risks and rewards of childhood freedom, and why the past may not deserve our rose-colored nostalgia. The following is a transcript of the episode: Meghan Cox Gurdon: I would say that parents today would be arrested for half the things—for almost anything that we were allowed to do. I mean, it is quite extraordinary. The social norms were so different back in the day. [ Music ] David Frum: Hello, and welcome to The David Frum Show. I’m David Frum, a staff writer at The Atlantic. And for this Thanksgiving edition of The David Frum Show , I’ll be talking to Meghan Cox Gurdon, author of a new memoir of growing up in the 1970s, Free Range Girl. At the end of the show, I’ll offer some personal words of thanks to you, the viewers and listeners of The David Frum Show. But before either the conclusion thanks or the dialogue, I want to talk at the beginning about why I invited Meghan Cox Gurdon to come and discuss her memoir of life in the 1970s. I was inspired by a 2026 poll conducted by NBC News that found that nearly half of adults ages 18 to 29 said that, if they had the option, they would choose to live in the past. They didn’t mean the ancient past. They didn’t mean horse-and-buggy days. They meant the recent past: the 1970s or the 1990s, about which they have all kinds of nostalgic feelings. So I wanted to tell them: I was there, and while definitely, like, the dating apps are making things worse and social media is a nuisance and AI is a little menacing, you do not wish you were there. You just don’t remember. I remember during the birther controversy of the Obama years when people had this fantasy that President Obama was born in Kenya. Remember that? Now, we know that President Obama’s mother was present in Hawaii, attending school, in the spring of the year that he was born, 1961. The theory of the case was that she somehow got from Hawaii to Kenya to give birth to the president and came back. But I took my first airplane flight in the middle 1960s with my parents, and I can remember some of those flights. I just want to conjure up what it would have been like for the young mother of President Obama to do this. I imagine a travel agent saying to her: Very well, Ms. Dunham, here’s your ticket. Honolulu to Los Angeles; Los Angeles to New York; New York to London; London to Nairobi. The Honolulu–Los Angeles leg of the trip by itself —and I looked this up— will cost more than a semester’s tuition at the University of Hawaii. You’ll have to pay by cash or certified check, since it’s exceedingly unlikely you qualify for American Express or Diners Club, as no other credit card yet exists. Bring plenty to read, since the in-flight movie has also only just been invented. I see you’re nine months pregnant, so you might ask the stewardess to seat you beside a passenger who doesn’t smoke. I hope your life insurance is up to date, since the risk of passenger fatality per mile is nearly 1,000 times greater than it will be in 2026. I mean, what were they thinking? How would that be? But they don’t remember. They don’t remember the world before seat belts. They don’t remember the world of universal smoking. I don’t even understand quite how any of us who were children in the 1960s and ’70s got out alive. One of the defining experiences of our childhoods was riding in a front seat beside an adult, and when a car in front of you braked, the adult would fling out an arm. ( Laughs. ) As if somehow their arm would stop you from crashing into the hard metal headboard that would otherwise bash you in. The past is a fascinating place. It’s full of interesting things to study. But you really don’t want to live there, and Meghan Gurdon and I will discuss why not in the segment that we’re about to begin. [ Music ] Frum: In 1976, the year America turned 200, a 12-year-old girl left her mother’s home in New York and moved to rural Maine to live with her father. He was a back-to-the-land man, and he had built the house himself. There was no hot water. The little girl bathed in a tin tub and carried spring water in by the bucket to heat on the stove. That year, the girl rode horses bareback, and one of them threw her. She was found face down in a field with a concussion and two black eyes. She burned her eyebrows off lighting an oven while babysitting her little cousin. The girl was Meghan Cox Gurdon. She grew up to become a foreign correspondent, and since 2005 she has been the children’s book critic of The Wall Street Journal . She is the author of The Enchanted Hour , about why reading aloud matters. Her new book is the story of that year in Maine in 1976. It’s called Free Range Girl. The book is about freedom, and also about what freedom costs; a childhood without screens or supervision among adults who are often busy with their own lives. We hear a lot of arguments about how today’s children are raised. Meghan has lived on both sides of that argument—first as the child in the story, and then as the parent of five children herself. Meghan, welcome to the show. Meghan Cox Gurdon: Thank you, David. I’m delighted to be with you. Frum: All right, so let’s start with the story of that year in 1976. Tell us what you left, what you went to, and how it happened. Gurdon: Well, actually, this is one of the interesting mysteries when you go back into the past to interrogate what happened, and when and why. It’s often quite difficult to put the puzzle pieces together. So in Free Range Girl , what I have done is I have represented what I understood at the time to be the case. So I had been living with my mother in a variety of towns and villages around upstate New York and Western Massachusetts since my parents divorced in 1970. And we often had housemates—it was a kind of improvisational, 1970s nomadic sort of childhood with a single mother. And in 1976, my father had moved back to the land up in Maine perhaps a year or so earlier, and it was announced to me that I would be going to live with him for the next year. And now, why that was—I think it’s not necessarily a known thing. But at the time I was told that it was so that I could get to know my father better. And in the way of children, I took the explanation that was given to me, and off I went. I packed my things up, including my bicentennial quarters, you know? Oh, because we had special bicentennial issues of everything back then. And I packed them all up into boxes, put them into the back of my father’s van, and he drove me up to Maine, which at the time seemed beyond everything. Like, you got across the border from New Hampshire into Maine, and it was like civilization ended. And that wasn’t true, of course; it’s a highly civilized place. But it seemed that way. Lots of trees, a lot of silence, not a lot of lights, not a lot of buildings. And that was my new reality. Frum: We belong to the generation of parents who kept a very close eye on our children, and I think it’s a little hard for those who are any younger than us to remember just how little attention was paid to children of our generation who grew up in the 1970s. You tell this story in a kind of very direct way, as you say. You tell what the child knew, not what the adult knows. But how unsupervised were you? How free-ranging were children allowed to be in the 1970s? Gurdon: Well, I would say that parents today would be arrested for half the things—for almost anything that we were allowed to do. I mean, it is quite extraordinary. The social norms were so different back in the day that you didn’t even have to—in 1976, you didn’t have to wear a seat belt. The whole world was less security-oriented, less safety-oriented, so all of childhood was less safety-oriented. You didn’t wear a helmet when you rode bikes, necessarily. You certainly didn’t when, in my case, when you were riding on horseback. People didn’t wear helmets when they were skiing. It was just a completely different, less safety-oriented time. And as a child, you were both given immense freedom to make mistakes. And, for example, you alluded to the blowing off of my eyebrows and eyelashes. That was when I had misunderstood how a gas stove worked. It was not a fatal injury. It was quite a useful injury in some ways. And I do think I agree with people like Jonathan Haidt who say that a certain amount of adversity in childhood does actually develop a child to be more resilient. It’s almost a meme now in the culture that if you grew up in our generation, you just kind of take things, you just sort of roll with it, and younger people are encouraged to be more fragile. And that’s regrettable, but the world has changed a lot. Frum: I remember I attended what Canadians call junior high school, what Americans know as middle school: [grades] seven, eight, and nine. And at my junior high school, middle school—so these are children who are 13, 14, 15, not even 16—there was a teachers’ parking lot. And just next door to it, there was this big hydroelectric box, a relay station, which was just off, was on the province’s land; not on the school’s land. And the 13-, 14-, 15-year-olds would go to the box and smoke cigarettes. And because the school’s view is once you are off school property and onto some other level of government’s property—and it wasn’t illegal for 13-, 14-, and 15-year-olds to smoke cigarettes—and the school would do nothing, and there’d be a crowd of kids standing around the green box smoking cigarettes, and no one thought anything of it. And the parents who could see it, because they would come to the teachers’ parking lot to pick up the kids, they would see that it was just, No, that’s where the smokers stood. Gurdon: So okay, so perhaps we today really look askance at smoking, and certainly smoking among the young. But there is a kind of experimental quality to that age, anyway. And one of the things I think that really helped us as young people was that we were sort of allowed—we were given a little running room to experiment long enough to have some real-world reactions to things. Smoking—okay, the analogy doesn’t go that far, but if you think about, like, climbing things and falling off them, if you fell at the park—I wasn’t ever taken to parks because that involved too much probably parental involvement. But I gather, at school, you fall off the monkey bars. They were these metal bars, and you fell off them onto asphalt. You learned how to hang on. And in fact, the epitaph for Free Range Girl comes from Charlotte’s Web. There’s a wonderful scene in Charlotte’s Web where E. B. White is writing about the Zuckermans’ barn. I don’t know if you remember this scene. But the Zuckermans’ barn is where Charlotte the spider and Wilbur the pig live, and this little girl, Fern, and her brother are on the swing. And E. B. White writes: Mothers from miles around feared that swing in Zuckerman’s barn . It’s just one of these enormous swinging things. And here’s the epitaph: But children always hold on more tightly than their parents think they will. And I think that’s something that we have forgotten. I think that is something that subsequent generations of parents have forgotten—that children do hold on more tightly. If you fall off the monkey bars, you hold on more tightly next time. If you blunder in one way or another, you learn. You become less fragile. You learn from adversity. Frum: So I have a number of things I want to go through with you. I want to start with the writing of the book, then about your experiences, and then to talk about this dialogue between the ages, then and now. So let’s start with the writing. You, the human being who wrote the book, know the 50 years of history since 1976. But you, the author of the book and the character in the book, know a lot less than you, the human being. So how did you purge all the things you know about the adult world, about humanity—first as an author and then as a character? How did you roll it back? Gurdon: I, actually, I would say I spent probably the first year that I was working on the book just working on it in my head, just trying to think. I was trying to decide: Should it be present tense, past tense? Should it be first person or third person? Should I put in gory details or leave out the gory details? Should I explain how things worked that were commonplace at the time and now unheard of, like a party line, you know? Eventually we got phone service at my father’s homestead, and we had a party line. Now, people of my generation know what that is, but people of, let’s say, who were born yesterday are not necessarily going to know what an artifact like that is. So— Frum: What is it? Gurdon: What is a party line? Oh, it’s—you don’t have a single dedicated phone line off your property. So you have a phone line that is shared with your neighbors or other parties. And so what would happen is, if you wanted to make a local call, you would pick up the receiver. And if you heard a dial tone, then you could call the local call, and if you heard voices, that meant that somebody else already had dibs on the phone line. And you would wait. It was not considered impolite, you know, to check maybe 30 seconds or a minute later, you know? And people who were having the conversation on the party line, the parties on that line, they would experience a little click—and they could kinda hear a hollow sort of sound that would tell them that some neighbor was trying to phone out. And that was for local calls. I mean, it’s so far away now. These were phones that were attached to the wall, an immovable object. Also, if you wanted to make a long-distance call—this again was from rural Maine, and maybe not the case everywhere in the country in 1976—you had to dial an operator in a nearby town, and the operator would connect you to your party. And there was no voicemail. You couldn’t leave a message. So if you just got a ringing tone on the other end, you had to call back later. I mean, it was just far away. Anyway, so, to go all the way back, so these are some of the questions that I was noodling over. And I would say it took me about a year to think about how I was going to approach it and also which stories to include, and what should the timeline be? Should it be the course of a single year, you know, 12 months of a single year? Should it be 12 chapters? How do you do it? Should it take place over several years? So at the end of all of that cogitation was the decision that I made to write the book in the third person, and my goal here was to just to try and capture what it was like back then. And yeah; so I wrote it in the third person, and that allowed me to get a little bit of kind of storytelling distance. It was more like I had the idea, maybe it would be something that would be very digestible for young people to read. I wasn’t exactly writing for a young audience. I was more writing something that could be read by young people as well as older people. So creating a time capsule that would be accessible to others. And then later on in the process, the pressure came from outside; my agent and my husband and various other people said, You know, you should really think about putting this in the first person. So it went from me writing about myself, Meg, a character, to writing the I: I did this, I did that . You know, and the remove of time is sufficient that I—the whatever I am, woman in her early 60s, you know, 50 years away from the events of I, the 12-year-old—I mean, every cell in my body I think has been replaced since then. So I’m like George Washington’s axe, you know? Is any part of me actually the person who was there? Yeah, memory, I guess; that part of me is there. Frum: Well, I talked about this dialogue between the girl in the book, the author inside the book, the author outside the book. There’s another dialogue that I think—and this, I think, will be the power of the book to people who don’t remember our generation. There’s a dialogue between the girl in the book and what she thinks is okay and normal. The author, you, outside the book, and your idea of what is okay and normal, which is pretty robust. And the child takes everything for granted. You, the author, have a pretty robust view, and then many of the readers of this book will say, “Good God, that went on in 1970?” Gurdon: ( Laughs .) I know. Frum: That’s how? How did Mom or Gra—how did they live to see this day? I look back on the period and think, How did anybody escape that period alive? Gurdon: As a 12-year-old—and maybe this is true of all children through all time, I don’t know—but the things I was; I was a bit of a scaredy-cat, I think, actually. There were things that frightened me. I was very worried, for instance, about vampires. I had a very serious fear of vampires. Which I, of course, fed by reading vampire books like Stephen King’s Salem’s Lot and Dracula itself, the original book. Fun fact: By the way, the front cover of Free Range Girl shows a little cottage or a little house in the woods in wintertime, and there’s smoke coming up from it, and there are words in the smoke. Those words come from Bram Stoker’s Dracula , because it really exerted this huge power on me. Anyway, I was afraid of vampires. I was afraid of grizzly bears, which do not exist in Maine. I was afraid of spiders. I was afraid—my cousin and I found a severed pig’s head in the woods, and we were afraid of that. I was afraid it was going to get me. Frum: That is pretty scary. Gurdon: But the things that actually, you know, now as a parent or grandparent as I am now, the things that actually represent a menace to a child of that age—like strangers, or going bareback without a helmet on a 16-hand-high horse at high speeds, riding the Greyhound bus by myself between Maine and Boston. Or even parental divorce. Which represent—and, like, a sequence of boyfriends involved with my mother. Those things represent actual danger. But the child of 1976 was far more worried about, you know, Barnabas Collins coming out of the shadows. Frum: Right. Well, the great thing about vampires was they obeyed very rigid rules. They couldn’t come in your house unless you somehow were tricked into giving them permission. Gurdon: That’s right. That’s true. I mean, you’re absolutely right, but I’m not sure as a 12-year-old that I was kind of really alive to the possibility that I could protect myself. So, at the point at which I was most afraid of being intercepted by a vampire. Which is, again, one of these things that just—I mean, lots of people have grown up in rough ways one way or another. When I would have to tiptoe out to the outhouse in the dark, and then I was terrified that a vampire—I would be sitting there in the dark, vulnerable, and the door would fly open, and a vampire would be standing there. I mean, there’s some sublimated weirdness here. But a vampire would be standing outside, with his cape rippling in the moonlight, and then he’d get me. That was probably my most intense fear at the time. It was—I mean, it was a lot to adapt to. Also, you know, going from flush toilets and hot and cold running water that just came out of the wall—you would just turn a tap and it would just come out—to an entirely different world where nothing was automatic. I mean, to heat water—as you mentioned at the beginning—to heat water, the wood had to be chopped and stacked and dried, and then it had to be carried into the kitchen. And we had two mechanisms for burning wood. One was a heat stove, which was used in the winter always, and there was also a cook stove, which was used even in the summer. Which was really, I mean, it was like something from Little House on the Prairie. It was this beautiful cast-iron thing with a little firebox on the left. And in order to, you know, heat water, you, again, did not turn a tap in the wall. You had to haul water from the spring in a bucket, and put it on the stove, in a vessel of some kind having started a fire in the firebox. And it was laborious, and it was kind of absurd in a way. I mean, you didn’t, we didn’t have to live this way. You know, in the 19th century you did, but by the 20th century you really didn’t. It was partly an expression of my father’s romanticism. I think he really admired that way of that sort of self-sufficient life, of Thoreau and people of that ilk. But it was also—there was a lot of tactile pleasure in it. And one of the things I really wanted to capture when I started writing Free Range Girl is how very different the world was when you had physical feedback from almost everything all the time. We are accustomed to, habituated now, to these smooth movements—smooth surfaces interfacing infinitesimally fast. Actually, that’s the wrong term, but you know what I mean. Like, so quickly; there’s no delay with anything that we want. We can swipe right, we can swipe left, we can swipe up, we can scroll. And it just wasn’t like that then. Everything had a knob. Everything had a switch, or it had an actual latch that you had to unlift. So there were compensations for the peculiar primitive nature of it all. Frum: This wasn’t Little House on the Prairie, which is—your choice was living in a tenement in a city and being a manual worker or having some land of your own and still being a manual worker, but at least owning the fruits of your labor, and so that was attractive. These are people who—you could live in Boston and have hot water instantly, and you choose not to. And one of the things I look back on is to say: How do we explain the adults of 1975 and ’76 who are so, by our contemporary standards, so neglectful? So heedless of the dangers that their children were incurring? Gurdon: Okay, so just this morning, knowing I was going to talk with you, I was thinking a little bit about this. One of the things that Free Range Girl has done, one of its effects that I was hoping it would do, is it causes people who read it to reflect on their own childhoods. And I’ve been hearing extraordinary stories from friends of mine. So I would say—so here I am, divorced parents kind of living for themselves, and I’m sort of tagging along, fitting in. But there were parents who adhered to the old script, who stayed married, who maybe prioritized the cocktail hour and getting dressed and going to the country club and whatever. And they, too—there was a kind of neglectful fecklessness about those people, too. I heard an extraordinary story this weekend from a friend of mine who said that her parents—you know, they had stayed married. They were very organized. They lived in comfort in Chicago. And they were having a cocktail party one night, and something caught on fire in the kitchen. And so the fire department was called, and everybody was hustled out of the apartment. And one of the firemen said to my friend’s mother, she said, the fireman said, Is there anyone else in the apartment? And she said, Just the cat. Totally forgetting her two daughters who had been put to sleep in the bedroom. So, I don’t think it was just the back-to-the-landers who were, who just—I know you’ve written about the ’70s extensively. There was a kind of real prioritization of “me”— me being the self-actualizing adult. So the adult might think, I want to live a glamorous life and, you know, have cocktail parties. And that was valorized and allowed. Or the adult might say, I want to be freed from the constraints of marriage. I want to really experience my independence, my intellect, my sexual autonomy, whatever. And they also misbehaved with regards to children. Frum: Alcohol was a factor back then, too, in a way that’s very hard for people who live a kind of normal bourgeois life to imagine today. About how—that woman who forgot the two kids. You put yourself in that situation; you think, Oh, how, how could she forget? Well, she probably had more drinks in that evening than her counterpart today would have in a week. Gurdon: Right. And also cigarettes, remember? Of course, they don’t addle the mind quite so much. But do you remember back in the day, it was just everything smelled like cigarettes all the time. And every place you went, there were cigarettes; there were ashtrays. There were ashtrays in cars. There were, as you had experienced at school, there was a completely acceptable kind of middle-school smoking, behind-the-gym kind of thing. We can’t celebrate that age too much. It’s very easy to look back with nostalgia, because when you’re young, the world is fresh and exciting, and those things seem very distinct. You know, was it more fun for parents? Possibly. Maybe. Frum: Well, you and I, I think, have slightly different views. I think you, because of your robust attitudes toward child-rearing—I look back on the age with total horror. I have no nostalgia. If I could send, if I could put United States Marshals in time machines and send them back in time, I would do so. That’s obviously not feasible. But the one place where I have some sympathy—I’ve been writing about this; I’ve been working on a memoir for a while myself. And the one thing I’m looking back on that age where as we were just, as we know, everyone was—the adults were engaging in sexual autonomy and splitting up. My parents who stayed together until my mother’s death would say that they felt like the characters in the movie The Last Married Couple in America— well, they were in Canada. I mean, everybody was getting divorced, and they weren’t. And it’s almost like, What was wrong with you? And I think back on it. So the people of my parents’ generation, I think yours: They were children during the Depression. They were too young for the war. But they were pulled as, I mean, there was this tremendous shortage of young people in the world of the 1950s. And so they were pulled, like, by this wind tunnel of advancing pressure into adulthood at an extraordinarily early age. So people now say, Well, wow; back then, you know, by the time you were 30, you owned a house. Yeah, by the time you were 30, you owned a house, and you were married, and you had kids, and they’re six and seven years old. And then you suddenly were 30, and you had married this person at, if you’re a woman, at 19, 20, 21. If you’re a man, at 23, 24, 25. You had two kids, maybe three under the age of 10. You did own a house, but you had a mortgage. You were in a job, and you were a full-blown adult at age 32. And you thought, Where was my youth? Gurdon: And then you suddenly have a culture springing up, of liberation springing up around you. Or what was called liberation, probably about as— Frum: And one more thing, which is, so if you are our parents—my father was born in 1931, and my mother was born in 1937. Nobody’s born in those years. I mean, it was the Depression. Then suddenly—so now you’re 32, and the world is full of all of these 20-somethings born in 1946, ’47, ’48, ’49, ’50, ’51. Young people of the opposite sex, very footloose, who are having a youth. And you think, Why did God decide that I was going to be a junior partner in an accounting firm at age 32, with a house, yes, and kids—and there are all these young people around who are having much more fun than I was ever allowed to? Now is my turn. And those two kids of mine, they’re going to pay on the front end what I paid on, what I’m paying, to make up for what I lost on the front end . Gurdon: Yeah, I think there was a lot of reassuring propaganda around children at that time. I think you’re being generous to the parents who were deciding to dissolve their marriages in their 30s and 40s at that time. And that they would imagine that their children were paying. I think one of the great lies of the era was this notion that children would be better off, that everybody’s better off, if mother and father do not live together anymore. Mom will be happier, Dad will be happier, and kids will be happier too, because they’ll be in a conflict-free home, and they’ll see what authentic love is when their parents meet other people. I mean, obviously, not every divorce was a catastrophe. I know of a number of divorces in which things worked out really beautifully. And so one can’t make a blanket statement. But I think for a lot of us—it was not myself, but others who have read Free Range Girl said, This is a divorce book, really. And honestly, I wrote it. But as Tom Stoppard once said about his plays when people were finding leitmotifs in them, he said, Well, I can see that they’re there, but I didn’t put them in myself. It’s a little like that. I don’t think of myself as having written a divorce book, but it was all over childhood. Frum: Let’s ourselves go through this veil of ignorance and do the exercise you did, and go back to that time—because you are making here an implicit case: We really have lost things . So what did Meg in the book have that a modern Meg might reasonably, and while keeping her eyebrows— Gurdon: Yeah. ( Laughs .) Frum: Might wish she had? Gurdon: You know, I think that there was an—you, as a child. I can speak only for myself here; obviously there are many types of children and people, and I was a kind of cheerfully oblivious bookworm. And I was an only child. Therefore, I didn’t share anything. I had no distractions. I had no other people, and I had an immense amount of free time. And the time was not merely free and unscheduled; it was also, it was sort of mentally, intellectually free. I simply didn’t have any cluttering in my head. And this is, I think, one of the greatest differences between then and now; that before the internet, there was simply no alternate reality. Clearly, you could think about the past; you could think about the future; you could imagine yourself in a different place; you could imagine stories that you’d seen on movies or television or in a book or whatever. So to that degree, there has always been available to the human mind an alternate reality. But what we have now is so profoundly different. And has changed us, I think, so much, that even when you are untethered from technology now, you are alive to the existence of technology a mere short distance away. You just go into the next room. I mean, it’s great that you and I can talk like this—thank you, technology—but it has also, I think, affected our ability to be in time the way that we used to be in time. So that is something I think that Meg of the past really—I mean, this all sounds so clichéd, because everyone’s talking about it now, talking about childhood then and now. But it is really true that there are blessings in a skinned knee, and there is a blessing in downtime where you have to just be in your own head, and there’s no entertainment, and there’s nothing else around. There’s no other way for people to contact you. You’re just in the moment. And there was a kind of autonomy about this. So I mentioned earlier about not wearing a helmet when I rode horseback. That is actually one of the things that shows the trade-offs to me, the loss and gain. So if you wear a helmet, you are a lot safer if you are thrown from your horse and your head hits the asphalt. I mean, no question. You might not go to the hospital for a week, as I did back in the day. But if you don’t wear a helmet, you have the whole sky over your head. You have all the birdsong in your ears. You feel the breeze stirring your hair. There’s a kind of aesthetic, natural pleasure that you get from being unprotected, that it’s obliterated if you are protected. And I think we can extrapolate out from that in all kinds of directions. If you have to get yourself from point A to point B and no grown-up is going to drive you, then you’re walking on the side of the road, okay. You know, you could get hit by a car. Something bad could happen. Also, there’s the wind, there are the leaves, there are the flowers, there’s the crunch of the ground under your feet. So you’re getting a lot, as well as losing things. Frum: One of the things I remember being struck by, especially with our youngest children when the smartphones began to circulate, was meeting kids of 10 and 11 years old who had no idea where they were, or how to get from where they were to a store five or six blocks away by themselves. Gurdon: Yeah. Actually, my husband tells an amazing story. When he was seven, my husband’s father, my father-in-law, he was a little concerned that little Hugo wasn’t showing enough autonomy or whatever. I think he was mistaken, but anyway. So he got my husband, who was then seven, up out of bed in the morning, drove him a couple of miles away from where they lived, and made him get out of the car. He said, Find your way home. ( Laughs .) Because he was concerned that his seven-year-old child would—so, you know, it’s a really interesting thing. I mean, so okay, in the Laura Ingalls Wilder books, there’s a very bad boy. People who’ve read those books will remember this. He’s a child who—oh, Charlie, I think his name is—he will not obey his father. His father bosses him around, and the kid won’t obey. And you see in the story of Charlie in this particular book: So Charlie is misbehaving in the field, he’s supposed to be working. He’s gambling about, and he steps on a hornet’s nest, and he’s horribly stung, and it’s a great morality tale. And I think that parents in the way-past were pretty careful to try and inculcate in their children a kind of obedience to voice commands for exactly that reason. Because there was a lot of danger out there. Or making sure that your children can find their way home. Like, what if he gets lost? Well, he’s got to find his way home. You’re right; those are skills, those things. Finding yourself in the universe and getting— Frum: There was also, in your book and in my memory, there was no homework. This is something that I remember: the first time I encountered homework. I transitioned schools in the middle of 10th grade. I went to a kind of, it wasn’t exactly a pri—it was like a lab school. It was affiliated with the University of Toronto; it was in the public system, but outside the public rules. And it was the first time I’d ever encountered homework before. It was a shocking imposition that you would come home, that your time was not your own when you came home from school. And I cannot remember before 10th grade ever having homework. And young Meg in the book, she doesn’t have any homework. Gurdon: Oh, she does. There’s one incident; you might remember this. I was assigned a term paper. It was called a term paper, and it had— Frum: Yes. Gurdon: And it had footnotes. It was so exciting. But you know, I typed my term paper on an old Underwood typewriter that my grandfather had bought at a tag sale and refurbished. You really had to use a lot of finger strength to get those things to click, to click the letters. But you’re right. Otherwise, there—you say imposition. That’s right. When you got home, you were in this other reality. You had just your, maybe your chores to do, maybe a local friend you would see. You were just basically on your own. You weren’t still working for school. You weren’t still accountable to people from school. There was no group chatting. There was no checking your Insta and your Finsta and any of that. That—speaking of impositions—is a real imposition on adolescents, young adolescents today. I mean, there’s a sense in which they have to serve the internet in order to fit in with their peer groups. We didn’t have to do that. Frum: And the adult certainly would never consider helping you with homework. It wouldn’t occur to anybody; it wouldn’t occur to the child to ask, or the adult to do. Gurdon: No. I did make the mistake of asking my father for help with math once or twice. He was a very hot-tempered guy in those days, and he couldn’t—I’m one of those people for whom math only ever made sense, the thing we were learning only made sense when it was too late. Like the next week you would learn; I don’t know. Like, see, I don’t even know enough about math to explain what I didn’t know. But the scales would fall from my eyes a little too late to fix my grade. So I was always a little behind. For instance, I did not, or no one told me, I just did not understand that division was the opposite of multiplication. So I made the mistake of asking my father a couple of times for help with math. And then I didn’t, because he got so cross with me for being such a dolt. Frum: And then we became adults, and there we were helping our children to make models of Independence Hall or Windsor Castle or something out of Play-Doh or flour. Gurdon: Yeah. Or the terrible thing where they would say to you, at 8 o’clock on a Sunday night: Oh, by the way, I need a tri-board and paint by tomorrow, ’cause I have to do a project for tomorrow morning about the weather. The cycle of rain and evaporation or whatever. And then you’d have to hustle out to the local drugstore and buy the tri-board. Tri-boards, we didn’t have tri-boards in 1976. Maybe we did. I had a deprived upbringing. There were probably children who were having a very deluxe time, and their mothers had to run out and get tri-boards at 8 o’clock on a Sunday, but not mine. I mean, my parents wouldn’t even drive me anywhere. The idea that an adult would—as is customary today—that an adult would structure his or her day around the need to transport children at a time of the child’s convenience was, I would say, that was pretty much generally unheard of. Even parents who were more attentive to their children, children I knew back in the day—if you wanted to go to town for something, you wanted to go to the store for something, you kind of had to hitchhike along with some other adult, not even necessarily in your own household, who was going to go and do that thing. And if you wanted to go to the store at 2 o’clock in the afternoon, but the ride was leaving at 1 o’lcock, you left at 1 o’clock. I mean, the idea that your convenience would come first, would supersede an adult’s convenience, was just—it was fantasy. Frum: So how does this end for Meghan, the book? She is going to return to the city someday. How does that happen? Gurdon: So I can’t tell you, because it would spoil the ending of the book. But I will say that at the ending of the book, after having had this experimental year in Maine, this poor little only child from a broken home has to make a big decision about where she’s going to live, and her decision is what ends the book. And forgive me for being coy, but I hate to blow up the ending. Frum: Then let me ask you to widen out the aperture and tell me the social ending. How does this world that you describe—when do you think that comes to an end? When do parents start driving children to things? I can’t remember my parents, for example, ever attending a sporting event or a school play, and they were reasonably attentive parents. They’re—well, no, they weren’t attentive parents, but they were involved and caring and loving parents who stayed together. But they would’ve been shocked to be asked. I would never have asked, and no one else was there. But when does the world we know—where the parents, you know, the dress rehearsals, the parents are there? The soccer games, the parents are there. The chauffeur service begins. When does all of that get going, do you think? Gurdon: Yeah. I mean, you know, David, you probably have demographic answers to this. What I see is there are some various cultural influences that produced this world. One, there was a murder. It was really awful. A little boy in New York City, I think he was called Etan Patz, something like that, and he was a little guy, like six, seven years old. And it was his first day of school. And his mother, his parents agreed to let him walk a block to his school, and he never made it, and for many years his murder was unsolved. I think finally it was solved. But the death of that little child happened at the same time that we began to get 24-hour news. And then with access to 24-hour news, there was also the press of the news cycle in the home, on every person. You’re aware of things happening around the world. I mean, we’re so accustomed now to being absolutely connected to all things—and to be able to find out at a moment’s notice anything happening in any remote part of the world—that it does seem like ancient history. But there really was a time, and within living memory, when you would have to exert some effort to find out what was going on places. And therefore, so we had the growth of the 24-hour news—or the onslaught of 24-hour news—which needed to find material. If it bleeds, it leads, right? The old local-news saying. So I think that, I would call it the early ’80s is when things really began to shift. Frum: Do you think it was also when that generation of child who was the Meg of the book becomes a parent himself or herself, and says: You know, kind of wish my parents had been at the soccer game. I’m going to go ? Gurdon: Yeah; I think that may be so. That may well be so. I mean, I myself may be an outlier on this. I really—I, of course I wanted to go to my, or I felt that I should go, to my children’s things. But I will say for myself—I started having children in the late ’90s. And we moved, my husband and I moved our family back to the United States in 2000. Well, North America. Call it in 2000, something. I don’t know exactly. And I felt at that time that I was stepping into a fully formed parenting culture, and I was out of step with parenting culture. By 2000, parenting culture, it was very conciliatory. Children were given a lot of choices. Fathers would kneel down and say, How ya doing, buddy? to their children. You know, Okay, time to go. Okay, Daddy’s going to go to the car now. There was a real softening of parental authority, and there was also a great focus on what we now would call maxxing. So maxxing the nutrition value of the foods that your children ate; maxxing the time, the out-of-school extracurricular activities, you know. Again, when did it happen? My guess is probably somewhere between 1980 and 2000. By the time I got there in 2000—I already had a couple kids at that point—what seemed to me a very repressive and strangely adult abnegating culture had very much taken hold. Frum: Is there some way to capture what was liberating and free for Meg in the book while protecting the eyebrows, and head from concussion? Is there any way to get the best of—or are these just inevitable trade-offs? You have the freedom, and you have the danger; you have the safety, you don’t have the freedom. Can modern parents find some wisdom in the story of your book, to say—how do they get the best of this without the worst? Gurdon: So this is a hard question to answer. I would recommend a tradition we had in our family, and our tradition was called, If you can climb it, you can climb it. In other words, if there were an imposing wall or very tall trees, if a child could get up into the tree or up onto the wall, then the child was allowed to go. But we were not going to help you get up. So occasionally a child would say, Oh, I want to climb this maple tree. Can you help me get up on the first branch? And my rule was, No, I will not help you get up on the first branch. You have to show the tenacity that you can get up onto that branch. But if you get up onto that branch, you can climb as high as you wanna go. I would let them do that. Is that good advice? I don’t know. I do think that we suffocate children somewhat by preventing them from having adventures by themselves, taking risks by themselves, learning to hold on. You know, nagging them all the time: “Hold on. Don’t go too high.” You know, it’s such a bummer. Who wants to be told that all the time? It’s natural for children to try to seek, to strive, to learn from experience. You know, to get up on things. If even, if a roof can be got up onto, get up on the roof, you know? It’s—you could fall off, sure. But what you lose in preventing that kind of experimenting, it seems to me, is more than what you gain by preventing it. Frum: And the eyebrows grew back? Gurdon: The eyebrows grew. See, eyebrows grow back. Bones knit back together. Concussions—I don’t know if my concussion has given me lifelong problems. Probably. But also, it was a kind of, it was a big experience. And I think that it’s worth having. You remember there’s that line from the movie Finding Nemo —which is all on this theme, of course, of a highly protective father who feels that his son needs to be shielded from adversity. And there’s another fish character who says to the fish father—this worried fish father, he says, I’ll never let anything happen to you, to his son. And the other fish says: Well, that’s not much fun for him, is it? And that’s pretty much where I come down on it. Frum: The artless, in-the-moment way in which the book is written, that is actually your considered view of looking back on this time, and all the hazards, to say, You know what? The girl was right. Gurdon: You know, that is a bit difficult. I don’t think that I do really think that. I wrote about the past as it really was—partly as a tonic for the way that things are now, and partly just to try and bottle what it was like. It was a way of life. It was a degree of neglect that was really quite remarkable. And things that I saw when I revisited the past that I had not noticed going by, I represented as seen by the child with, I hope, some truth. There is, for example; you’ll remember, that winter of 1976 was very—there was a lot of snow, a lot of ice. It was a big, heavy winter in New England, and I didn’t have a winter coat. My father never thought to get me a winter coat. My mother, who was not living with me up in Maine and therefore not seeing me cold every morning, didn’t think to get me a winter coat. It simply didn’t occur to the adults who were in charge of me, and I was aware that money was tight, and so I just made do. And so people would ask me—I had a windbreaker, and I put a vest over the windbreaker. And I had mittens, but they didn’t quite meet the windbreaker sleeve, and the windbreaker sleeve got burned, and it was all a little bit haphazard. And people would say to me, Oh, aren’t you cold? And I’d say, No, I’m fine. Well, you know; that’s not true. And I don’t recommend that way of life. I think that if you can get a winter coat for your child, you ought to do it. So I’m not being prescriptive here. I’m being descriptive. I’m trying to be descriptive. I’m not so much condemning modern parenting and modern life as I am holding a mirror up to it. Frum: Well, I will say as a reader of Free Range Girl in both the galley and the printed form, that the literary achievement is you burn away everything that the adult world might know. And you just—you make us all remember what it was like, how our memories were when we were children, and the world was fresh and new, and everything was taken for granted. And just because it was the way it was, you couldn’t imagine any other way that it might be than the way it was. That all comes later. And just that direct immersive experience. And I think many people who read Free Range Girl will be prodded to think about their own childhood, whether it was in that era or a later era. And to say, just remembering how things were liberates you from the present. But remembering the present does cast some judgment on the past. ( Laughs .) But maybe the past more than amply deserved, if one were a child. Gurdon: Thank you. I think that’s right. And I mean, look—if the book gives readers a feeling that they have traveled a little in time, and if it causes them to reflect on their own childhoods, I would say mission accomplished right there. That is really what I was hoping to do. Frum: Well, Meghan, thank you so much for this talk, and thank you for Free Range Girl. And every success with the book, and have a great Thanksgiving. Gurdon: Thank you, David. Frum: Bye-bye. [ Music ] Frum: Thanks so much to Meghan Cox Gurdon for joining me today on The David Frum Show to discuss her memoir, Free Range Girl. It’s Thanksgiving tomorrow, so I want to say a word of my thanks on behalf of myself and the entire Atlantic video team for the support and enthusiasm you, our viewers and listeners, have shown since we launched this program a year and a half ago. The Atlantic has just passed a million subscribers to its YouTube channel, and we on this program have had more than 30 million views and downloads on YouTube and the audio platforms. We are so touched and grateful by this enthusiasm. I thank you for it. I hope to continue to justify it, and I hope you will share these programs if you enjoy them with friends and others who might also enjoy them. And to continue to show that the internet can be a place for discussion as we want it to be, not just discussion as we have to suffer it to be. I wish you all a joyous Thanksgiving with those you love best. See you soon here on The David Frum Show. Bye-bye.

items.title: Les autorités mobilisées pour une ville plus propre et plus accessible
items.description: La préfecture et la municipalité de Saint-Louis ont engagé une opération de désengorgement de l’espace public, prévue sur trois jours. L’initiative vise à libérer les principales artères de la ville des épaves de véhicules, des dépôts de gravats et des occupations irrégulières, afin de faciliter la circulation et d’améliorer le cadre de vie. À Saint-Louis, les autorités veulent redonner aux rues leur vocation première. Depuis hier, une opération de désencombrement est menée dans la commune pour débarrasser les voies publiques des obstacles qui entravent la circulation des personnes et des biens. Le préfet du département, Maurice Latyr Dione, explique que cette initiative fait suite à un constat d’occupation anarchique de certaines artères. « Les rues étaient occupées par des encombrants, soit des épaves de véhicules abandonnées depuis longtemps, soit des occupations du domaine public qui n’étaient pas conformes à la loi », a-t-il indiqué. L’opération, qui s’étend sur trois jours, concerne principalement la route nationale numéro 2, la digue de Ndiolofene et l’avenue Macky Sall. Les équipes mobilisées procèdent notamment à l’enlèvement d’épaves de véhicules, de tas de gravats et de débordements d’activités commerciales sur la voie publique. Pour le préfet, l’enjeu est aussi sécuritaire. « L’objectif, c’est justement de libérer les trottoirs et la voie publique pour permettre aux citoyens d’aller et de venir de façon libre, sans contrainte et sans obstacle », a-t-il souligné. Les véhicules abandonnés peuvent, selon lui, constituer des repaires pour des malfaiteurs ou présenter des risques pour les populations, notamment les enfants. L’opération a été préparée à travers des réunions de coordination impliquant les autorités administratives, la mairie et les services techniques concernés. Une phase d’évaluation est prévue à l’issue des interventions, suivie de la mise en place d’un dispositif de surveillance pour préserver les espaces libérés. L’adjoint au maire chargé du commerce, du transport et de la mobilité urbaine, Mayib Seck, s’est réjoui de cette initiative et a salué l’implication des autorités nationales et territoriales. Il a assuré que la municipalité veillera à la pérennité des résultats. « Nous sommes prêts pour le suivi », a-t-il déclaré, rappelant que les précédentes opérations de désencombrement n’avaient pas toujours permis de maintenir durablement les espaces dégagés. Les autorités appellent ainsi les commerçants et l’ensemble des habitants à faire preuve de civisme et à coopérer. « Nous ne le faisons pas pour empêcher les gens de travailler. Les gens peuvent travailler, mais sans entraver la libre circulation des personnes et des biens », a insisté le préfet. Jeanne SAGNA (Correspondante)

items.description: La Direction générale des élections (DGE) a publié ce mercredi 25 novembre 2026, par décision officielle, la liste provisoire des candidatures retenues pour la zone spéciale de Conakry. Le scrutin sénatorial est prévu le 20 décembre prochain. Selon le document, 50 candidatures ont été provisoirement pour les 13 communes de la capitale. La synthèse générale fait état de 71 dossiers reçus, dont 21 ont été rejetés. Plusieurs figures connues dans la course Parmi les prétendants figurent des personnalités bien connues de l'opinion : – Baidy ARIBOT , ancien ministre et ancien vice-gouverneur de la Banque centrale de la République de Guinée (BCRG) ; – Dre Hadja Fatou Sikhé CAMARA , ancienne directrice générale de l'hôpital national Donka ; – Ibrahim Kassus DIOUBATÉ , diplomate et ancien consul de la Corée du Sud en Guinée ; – Mamadouba Tos CAMARA , ancien maire de la commune de Matoto ; – Joachim Baba Millimouno , ancien coordinateur de la cellule de communication de l'UFDG (parti dissous). Le détail par commune (candidatures reçues, validées, rejetées) – Dixinn : 3 reçues, 3 validées, 0 rejetée – Gbéssia : 6 reçues, 4 validées, 2 rejetées – Kagbelen : 5 reçues, 4 validées, 1 rejetée – Kaloum : 5 reçues, 3 validées, 2 rejetées – Kassa : 4 reçues, 3 validées, 1 rejetée – Lambanyi : 3 reçues, 1 validée, 2 rejetées – Manéah : 4 reçues, 3 validées, 1 rejetée – Matam : 4 reçues, 2 validées, 2 rejetées – Matoto : 7 reçues, 5 validées, 2 rejetées – Ratoma : 8 reçues, 6 validées, 2 rejetées – Sanoyah : 3 reçues, 1 validée, 2 rejetées – Sonfonia : 9 reçues, 8 validées, 1 rejetée – Tombolia : 10 reçues, 7 validées, 3 rejetées Sonfonia compte le plus grand nombre de candidatures validées (8), devant Tombolia (7) et Ratoma (6). À l'inverse, Lambanyi et Sanoyah n'ont retenu qu'une seule candidature chacune. Dixinn est la seule commune où aucun dossier n'a été écarté. Tombolia enregistre le plus grand nombre de rejets (3). Cette liste est provisoire. La liste complète des candidats retenus figure dans le document officiel de la DGE.

items.title: L’Algérie va exporter des dattes vers le Bangladesh pour 2 à 5 dollars le Kg
items.description: Un nouveau débouché pour les dattes algériennes , à un prix intéressant. Le Bangladesh, soucieux d'assurer l’approvisionnement de son marché avant le mois de Ramadan 2027, a opté pour la filière algérienne. L'importation directe de dattes d'Algérie par le biais des secteurs public et privé a fait l'objet d’une réunion entre le ministre bangladais du Commerce, Khandakar Abdul Muktadir, et l'ambassadeur d’Algérie au Bangladesh, Abdelouahab Saidani, rapporte le journal local tbsnews.net . Des dattes algériennes pour le Bangladesh avant le mois de Ramadan Le diplomate a fait savoir à son vis-à-vis que l'Algérie est actuellement en pleine saison des dattes et dispose d'un stock important de ce produit, rappelant que le ministère algérien de l'Agriculture avait déjà transmis une proposition pour la fourniture de dattes au Bangladesh « à des prix compétitifs ». Un exportateur algérien privé a également proposé de fournir des dattes à un prix compris entre 2 et 5 dollars le kilogramme, transport inclus, a indiqué l’ambassadeur. Malgré la distance, les cargaisons de dattes algériennes pourraient atteindre les ports bangladais dans un délai de 20 à 30 jours si les procédures nécessaires sont achevées d'ici la semaine prochaine, a précisé M. Saidani. Celui-ci a aussi informé le ministre bangladais des nouvelles réglementations algériennes concernant l'exportation de produits halal. La datte algérienne proposée à un prix intéressant pour les exportateurs Le prix proposé semble intéressant, au vu de la moyenne des prix appliqués par les exportateurs algériens de dattes. En septembre dernier, l'agence Ecofin a rapporté, sur la base des données de la plateforme Trade Map, que l’Algérie est le premier exportateur africain de dattes, mais elle est distancée en recettes par la Tunisie qui exporte moins, à cause de l'écart entre les prix appliqués. Selon les chiffres dévoilés, les exportations de l’Algérie se sont élevées en 2025 à 185.000 tonnes de dattes et les recettes tirées de ces exportations sont de 184 millions de dollars, soit moins de 1 dollar par kilogramme. En revanche, la Tunisie, deuxième exportateur de dattes du continent, a tiré pendant la même année 347 millions de dollars de 147.000 tonnes exportées, soit 38.000 tonnes de moins et 163 millions de dollars de plus que l’Algérie. Suivant ces données, le prix moyen de la datte tunisienne était en 2025 de 2,3 dollars par kilogramme. L’article L’Algérie va exporter des dattes vers le Bangladesh pour 2 à 5 dollars le Kg est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: L’Afrique veut ancrer la culture de la qualité dans ses universités
items.description: Réunis à Saly du 25 au 27 novembre, des responsables et experts africains de l’enseignement supérieur prennent part à la troisième édition du Colloque international de Dakar sur l’assurance qualité (CIDAQ 2026). Les échanges portent sur les moyens de faire de la qualité une exigence permanente dans la gouvernance des établissements, les formations, la recherche et l’innovation, afin de renforcer la performance des systèmes universitaires et la reconnaissance des diplômes. MBOUR- Faire de l’assurance qualité un pilier de la transformation des universités africaines. C’est l’ambition portée par la troisième édition du CIDAQ 2026, ouverte le 25 novembre à Saly. Jusqu’au 27 novembre, les participants débattent des mécanismes permettant d’inscrire durablement la culture qualité dans les pratiques des établissements d’enseignement supérieur, de recherche et d’innovation. À l’ouverture, le secrétaire exécutif de l’ANAQ-Sup, le professeur Massamba Diouf, a présenté le bilan de l’institution. En dix ans, près de 2 000 procédures d’habilitation et d’accréditation ont été engagées, avec un taux d’achèvement supérieur à 99 %. En 2025 et 2026, près de cinquante établissements et plus de 300 programmes ont été évalués. Huit écoles doctorales et quatre centres de recherche ont également fait l’objet d’évaluations externes. « Ces données traduisent la place désormais occupée par l’assurance qualité dans notre système », a souligné le professeur Diouf. Il a également insisté sur le suivi des accréditations. « Une accréditation obtenue ne constitue pas une garantie définitive. Elle doit s’inscrire dans un cycle régulier de suivi, d’amélioration et de réévaluation », a-t-il expliqué. Représentant le ministre de l’Enseignement supérieur, de la Recherche et de l’Innovation, le professeur Malick Fall, conseiller technique, a inscrit cette ambition dans la Vision Sénégal 2050 et l’Agenda national de transformation du secteur (ANTESRI 2050). « Notre défi est de faire en sorte que la qualité ne soit plus seulement un dossier préparé pour les évaluateurs, mais une pratique quotidienne, partagée par tous », a-t-il déclaré. Il a mis en avant trois priorités, notamment l’adaptation des formations aux besoins professionnels, la promotion d’une recherche rigoureuse et la reconnaissance des qualifications en Afrique. « Un diplôme ne circule que si l’on fait confiance au système qui l’a délivré », a-t-il rappelé, plaidant pour des référentiels communs et des évaluations transparentes. Le colloque devra déboucher sur des recommandations concrètes, assorties d’engagements et de résultats mesurables. Cette ambition s’appuie sur l’accompagnement de plus de 500 structures et la dématérialisation des évaluations grâce à la plateforme E-ANAQ. Ainsi, L’ANAQ-Sup prépare également son Plan stratégique 2026-2030 et envisage d’intégrer l’intelligence artificielle dans ses pratiques, dans le respect de la transparence et de la protection des données. En outre,la coopération entre agences africaines devra, par ailleurs, consolider la confiance, faciliter la mobilité académique et favoriser la reconnaissance des diplômes. Autant de perspectives pour bâtir un enseignement supérieur africain plus performant et mieux reconnu. Ibrahima MBAYE ( Correspondant)

items.title: Disparitions en mer : l’interminable attente des familles sans nouvelles de leurs jeunes
items.description: « Nous sommes sans nouvelles de lui » : le jeune Mamadou Diallo peine à garder espoir de retrouver vivant son ami deux semaines après son départ pour l'Espagne dans une pirogue au large du Sénégal, où de nombreuses familles sont dans l'attente fiévreuse de signes de vie de leurs proches portés disparus en mer. L'ami du jeune boutiquier d'une vingtaine d'années avait embarqué le 9 novembre à Ngor, une commune côtière de Dakar, à destination de l'archipel espagnol des Canaries, affirme à l'AFP Mamadou Diallo. La pirogue transportait au moins plusieurs dizaines de personnes. Des milliers de personnes migrantes originaires d'Afrique de l'Ouest, en majorité des jeunes, tentent depuis des années de gagner clandestinement l'Europe en empruntant la périlleuse route de l'Atlantique, principalement vers les Canaries, à bord d’embarcations surchargées et souvent vétustes. Mais le phénomène s'est amplifié ces derniers mois, avec un nombre de départs en forte augmentation, depuis les côtes du Sénégal et de la Gambie principalement, et ayant déjà causé plusieurs drames, ont constaté des journalistes de l'AFP. Au moins 43 personnes ont ainsi péri dans le chavirement de leur pirogue le 6 novembre au large de Thieppe, dans le nord-ouest du Sénégal. « Efficacité réelle » À Yenne, une autre commune côtière près de Dakar, une pirogue a également fait naufrage après avoir heurté des rochers. L’embarcation a été retrouvée et au moins dix corps ont depuis été repêchés, a affirmé à l'AFP Oumar Sow, représentant du chef du village. Ce bilan n'a pas encore été confirmé par les autorités. À Ngor, l'inquiétude est vive depuis le départ de la pirogue le 9 novembre. « Il y avait au moins 30 jeunes de Ngor dans cette pirogue. La plupart sont de jeunes pêcheurs, mais il y avait aussi des mécaniciens et au moins un boutiquier », a déclaré à l'AFP un habitant de la localité sous couvert d'anonymat. « Une de mes clientes a deux de ses fils à bord. Elle est désemparée… », a témoigné à l'AFP un autre boutiquier de Ngor. Dans un communiqué diffusé mardi, l'ONG Action pour les Droits Humains et l'Amitié (ADHA) fait état de « la disparition de 172 personnes, principalement des jeunes » dans la pirogue partie le 9 novembre. « Au regard des moyens humains, financiers et institutionnels mobilisés depuis plusieurs années, l'État du Sénégal peut-il démontrer l'efficacité réelle de sa politique migratoire et son impact sur les causes profondes des départs ? », s'interroge l'ONG. À Ngor, la disparition de cette pirogue est au centre des discussions. Une image de l’embarcation avant le départ et accompagnée de la mention « AVIS DE RECHERCHE, PIROGUE SANS NOUVELLE », circule largement sur les statuts WhatsApp des habitants, a constaté un journaliste de l'AFP. D'autres scrutent également les vidéos publiées sur TikTok, où des migrants partagent régulièrement les images de leur arrivée sur les côtes espagnoles. Sans succès, pour l'heure. « Je crains le pire » Lundi, un avion de reconnaissance a décollé de Las Palmas, dans les îles Canaries, pour tenter de retrouver la pirogue, mais sans succès, a indiqué à l'AFP Oumar Diop, membre de la cellule de communication de Boza Fii, l'une des principales association d'aide aux personnes migrantes et à leurs familles au Sénégal. Un nouveau vol de reconnaissance est prévu mardi. Un officier de la marine nationale sénégalaise, contacté par l'AFP, dit avoir reçu de nombreux messages de personnes inquiètes, à la recherche d'informations sur l’embarcation. « Malheureusement, la marine ne sait pas où se trouve cette pirogue (partie de Ngor, NDLR). Et si, comme vous dites, elle est partie depuis le 9 novembre et qu'on est sans nouvelles, je crains que le pire ne soit arrivé », a-t-il dit à l'AFP. Le Sénégal est enlisé depuis des mois dans une crise économique et politique qui pèse sur le quotidien des Sénégalais. Pour une grande partie de la jeunesse qui peine à trouver des perspectives d'avenir, rejoindre l'Europe représente un eldorado, nourri aussi par les récits de ceux qui ont réussi « l'aventure », comme ils appellent ce périlleux voyage. Les pays européens ayant drastiquement restreint la délivrance de visas et renforcé les contrôles à leurs frontières, prendre la mer représente l'une des ultimes options. La rédaction avec l'AFP

items.title: David Lisnard réélu à la tête des maires de France en pleine course à l’Élysée
items.description: David Lisnard a ete reelu ce 25 novembre, avec 72,06 % des suffrages, a la presidence de l'Association des maires de France (AMF), a l'occasion de son 108e congres, qui se tient porte de Versailles, a Paris. « Je remercie chaleureusement tous les maires de France pour leur confiance. C'est un magnifique resultat qui nous permettra de toujours mieux faire entendre la voix des libertes locales, des realites du terrain, de l'avenir d'une France du concret et des solutions », a declare le maire de Cannes dans un message poste sur X. Devant les journalistes, celui-ci a souligne un « maximum de participations depuis 1989 ». Un taux qui, selon l'AMF, s'est etabli a 40,43 % . « C'est la defaite des intrigues, des ingerences […] des appareils », a-t-il estime, en renvoyant notamment a la proximite de l'election presidentielle. « On a vu des personnalites nationales qui ne s'etaient jamais interessees au sort des maires, ou a la vie de l'association, vouloir nous dire comment il fallait voter. Les maires ont montre leur independance, leur liberte », a-t-il insiste, en assurant representer « les voix de tous les maires » au-dela des clivages politiques, et en saluant dans ces ediles des « praticiens du quotidien ». Lisnard, un « phenomene d'automne » selon le RN L'actuel candidat de « Nouvelle energie » a l'elysee decroche ainsi un troisieme mandat, en tant que president benevole de la puissante association d'elus, apres ceux remportes en 2021 puis en 2023 . « S'il est elu, c'est parce qu'il a fait le job », a declare au Figaro un cadre de l'AMF. David Lisnard affrontait une autre figure de l'association, le maire UDI de Sceaux Philippe Laurent. Presente dans la presse comme le « nouveau troisieme homme » de la course a l'elysee, David Lisnard progresse dans les intentions de vote depuis le debut de l'automne, jusqu'a devancer, dans certains sondages, celui qui faisait jusqu'alors figure de favori a droite et au centre : edouard Philippe. Une progression qui fait visiblement grincer des dents du cote de Marine Le Pen, candidate du Rassemblement national (RN). David Lisnard, qui fait preuve d'un certain franc-parler, entend notamment recourir au referendum sur la question de l'immigration. Un proche de la candidate du RN a toutefois raille sa percee aupres de LCI, la qualifiant de « phenomene d'automne ».

items.title: Drone attacks kill at least 15 across Blue Nile
items.description: Drone attacks struck Ed Damazin and El Roseires on Tuesday evening, killing at least 15 people and injuring dozens, according to local sources. The Blue Nile Civil Society Initiative initially reported 15 people killed and 15 injured. It said 14 members of three families were killed when drones struck a residential area in El Saliha, west of Ed Damazin . Blue Nile government spokesperson Saif El Nasr Minallah later put the death toll at 16, including seven women and two children, with 22 people injured. The initiative subsequently revised its figures to 17 dead and 20 injured. The initiative reported that more than 40 suicide drones targeted Ed Damazin and El Roseires. Five people were injured in Ed Damazin and 10 in El Roseires, where strikes hit a public viewing hall called the Okasha Club and nearby homes. A soldier was also reportedly killed. In Ed Damazin, strikes reportedly hit the El Matar, Rayih Balak and El Saliha neighbourhoods, setting homes ablaze and targeting the headquarters of the Sudanese Armed Force’s 4th Infantry Division. ‘Authorities impose curfew’ The Blue Nile authorities announced a curfew from 22:00 to 05:00 and banned motorcycles, except those used by authorised security personnel. The Blue Nile Civil Society Initiative blamed the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N) for the attacks, calling for an investigation and accountability. The strikes come amid escalating fighting in Blue Nile, where RSF and SPLM-N allied forces have advanced around Sodari locality, Kurmuk, Geissan locality and Wad El Mahi, raising concerns about further attacks on Ed Damazin. items.title: Burkina: intensification des contrôles pour assainir les marchés de Dagouma et Toècé
items.description: (Manga, le 25 novembre 2026) La Direction régionale de l’Industrie, du Commerce et de l’Artisanat du Nazinon (DRICA-Nazinon) a conduit, ce mercredi, une opération de contrôle des prix et de la qualité des produits de grande consommation dans les localités de Dagouma et de Toècé, dans la province du Bazèga. Cette mission vise à veiller au respect de la réglementation commerciale et à renforcer la protection des consommateurs. Au total, 18 établissements commerciaux ont été contrôlés. Les vérifications ont permis de relever plusieurs irrégularités, notamment le défaut d’affichage des prix, des cas de spéculation ainsi que la commercialisation de produits prohibés. À l'issue des contrôles, un établissement commercial a été mis sous scellés. Une quantité importante de produits prohibés et périmés a également été saisie. Des amendes ont par ailleurs été infligées aux contrevenants. À travers cette opération, la DRICA-Nazinon entend renforcer la lutte contre les pratiques commerciales illicites, assainir les circuits de distribution et contribuer à la mise à disposition des consommateurs de produits conformes aux exigences de qualité. Elle invite, en outre, les populations à rester vigilantes et à signaler aux services compétents tout manquement à la réglementation commerciale.
